**Partitions.** Let $n\ge 0$ be an integer. A **partition of $n$** is a finite
weakly decreasing sequence $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ of positive
integers with $\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_k=n$. Its entries are the **parts** of
$\lambda$ and $k$ is the **number of parts**. For $n=0$ the only partition is
the **empty partition** $\varnothing$, the empty sequence with $k=0$; for
$n\ge 1$ one has $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_k\ge 1$ and
$k\le n$. We write $\lambda\vdash n$. Trailing zeros are not parts: a finite
sequence of nonnegative integers ending in $0$ is not a partition, so the
number of parts of $\lambda$ is determined by $\lambda$ and
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ is a different data type from
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k,0)$.

**English Young diagrams.** The **(English) Young diagram** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$[\lambda]:=\{\,(i,j)\;:\;1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le \lambda_i\,\}\subseteq\mathbb N\times\mathbb N,$$
where $i$ numbers the **rows** downward and $j$ numbers the **columns**
rightward. An element of $[\lambda]$ is a **node**, or box, of the diagram. Row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ carries $\lambda_i$ nodes, and column $j$ carries
$$\lambda'_j:=\#\{\,i: \lambda_i\ge j\,\}$$
nodes, a quantity that is $0$ beyond the last column (and for every $j\ge1$ when $\lambda=\varnothing$). Since a partition is weakly
decreasing, $[\lambda]$ determines $\lambda$: if $[\mu]=[\lambda]$, then row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ is row $i$ of $[\mu]$, so $\mu_i=\lambda_i$ for every $i$
and $\mu=\lambda$. In particular $[\varnothing]=\emptyset$, the empty diagram.

**Conjugation.** The **conjugate partition** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$\lambda':=(\lambda'_1,\lambda'_2,\dots,\lambda'_{\lambda_1}),$$
the sequence of column heights of $[\lambda]$, with $\varnothing':=\varnothing$
for the empty partition. This is again a partition of $n$, and
$[\lambda']$ is the transpose of $[\lambda]$:
for $1\le i\le\lambda_1$ and $1\le j\le k$,
$$(i,j)\in[\lambda']\iff j\le\lambda'_i\iff \lambda_j\ge i\iff (j,i)\in[\lambda].$$
Outside these bounds neither diagram contains the corresponding node; for the empty partition both diagrams are empty.
Conjugation is an involution, $\lambda''=\lambda$, because
$\lambda''_i=\#\{j:\lambda'_j\ge i\}$ counts the columns of $[\lambda]$ of
height at least $i$, that is, the columns $j$ with at least $i$ rows of length
$\ge j$, which by weak decrease is exactly the set of $j\le\lambda_i$. Thus
$\lambda\mapsto\lambda'$ is a bijection on the partitions of $n$, exchanging
the number of parts with the largest part for nonempty partitions.

**Size zero.** The symmetric group of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is
$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]) for every
$n\ge 0$, and we fix
$$S_0:=\operatorname{Sym}(\emptyset)=\{1\},$$
the trivial group; for $n=0$ the set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is empty and the group
acts trivially on every size-zero object below. This is the convention used
whenever the constructions of this page are read at $n=0$.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ with Young diagram $[\lambda]$, and let
$\mu\vdash n-1$ and $\nu\vdash n+1$ denote partitions of the neighbouring
sizes ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

A node $x\in[\lambda]$ is **removable** if deleting it leaves a Young diagram,
that is, if there is a partition $\mu\vdash n-1$ with
$$[\mu]=[\lambda]\setminus\{x\};$$
such a $\mu$ is unique because a partition is determined by its diagram. A
point $y\notin[\lambda]$ is **addable** for $\lambda$ if inserting it leaves a
Young diagram, that is, if there is a partition $\nu\vdash n+1$ with
$$[\nu]=[\lambda]\cup\{y\};$$
again $\nu$ is unique. We write $\operatorname{Rem}(\lambda)$ and
$\operatorname{Add}(\lambda)$ for the sets of removable and of addable nodes
of $\lambda$.

Since $[\lambda]=\{(i,j):1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le\lambda_i\}$ is determined by
the inequalities $1\le j\le\lambda_i$, the two conditions have the following
row form. Write $\lambda_{k+1}:=0$ for a partition $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$.
A node $(i,\lambda_i)$ is removable if and only if
$\lambda_i>\lambda_{i+1}$: deleting the last node of row $i$ keeps the row
lengths weakly decreasing exactly when row $i+1$ is strictly shorter, and no
node $(i,j)$ with $j<\lambda_i$ can be deleted, since the node
$(i,j+1)$ would then have no node to its left. Similarly a node
$(i,\lambda_i+1)$ with $1\le i\le k$ is addable if and only if $i=1$ or
$\lambda_{i-1}>\lambda_i$, the node $(k+1,1)$ opening a new row is always
addable, and these are all the addable nodes. In particular a row endpoint of
$[\lambda]$ is removable only if no node of $[\lambda]$ lies immediately
below it.

For the empty partition the diagram is empty, so
$\operatorname{Rem}(\varnothing)=\emptyset$, while
$\operatorname{Add}(\varnothing)=\{(1,1)\}$ is a single node, whose insertion
produces the partition $(1)$.

Let $p$ be a prime and let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition of $n\ge0$ with
parts $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_k\ge1$ and conjugate partition
$\lambda'$, whose $j$-th part is the number $\lambda'_j=\#\{i:\lambda_i\ge j\}$
of nodes of $[\lambda]$ in column $j$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For $j\ge1$ let
$$z_j(\lambda):=\#\{\,i:\lambda_i=j\,\}$$
be the multiplicity with which the positive integer $j$ occurs as a part of
$\lambda$; only finitely many $z_j$ are nonzero.

- $\lambda$ is **$p$-regular** when every positive part of $\lambda$ occurs
  fewer than $p$ times, that is, when $z_j(\lambda)<p$ for every $j\ge1$.
- $\lambda$ is **$p$-restricted** when $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<p$ for every
  $i\ge1$, where the sequence is padded by the trailing zeros
  $\lambda_i:=0$ for $i>k$.

Both conditions are finite families of inequalities. For $i>k$ one has
$\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}=0<p$, so the restrictedness condition is the finite
list for $1\le i\le k$. The empty partition $\varnothing\vdash0$ has no parts
and $k=0$, so $z_j(\varnothing)=0<p$ and $0-0=0<p$ for every $j,i\ge1$: it is
simultaneously $p$-regular and $p$-restricted for every prime $p$.

The two conditions are exchanged by conjugation: **$\lambda$ is $p$-restricted
if and only if $\lambda'$ is $p$-regular.** The number of columns of $[\lambda]$
of height exactly $i$ is the difference $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}$ of consecutive
parts, and these heights are precisely the parts of $\lambda'$, so the
multiplicity of the part $i$ in $\lambda'$ is $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}$; the
stated equivalence compares the same integers with $p$.

The names record two genuinely different label conventions used later on this
page: James's modular simple modules $D^\lambda$ are labelled by **$p$-regular**
$\lambda$. Dual Specht modules themselves are defined for every partition;
their simple heads give the **$p$-restricted** labelling of simple modules,
related to the first convention by transposition and a sign twist. Neither
class of partitions contains the other in general.

Let $F:=\bigoplus_{\lambda}\mathbb Q(q)|\lambda\rangle$ be the charge-$0$ part of
the Fock space of
[[lem-semi-infinite-wedges-are-indexed-by-partitions-and-give-node-action-formulas]],
with basis indexed by all partitions and with the node operators $F_i,E_i$
defined by the stable finite-prefix action. Assign to $|\lambda\rangle$ the
**level-one weight**

$$\mathrm{wt}(|\lambda\rangle):=\Lambda_0-\sum_{i\in I}m_i(\lambda)\,\alpha_i, \qquad m_i(\lambda):=\#\{\text{cells of }\lambda\text{ of residue }i\},$$

where the **residue** of a cell in row $r$ and column $c$ is $c-r\bmod e$, and
the **size** $|\lambda|$ is the separate grading. The vacuum is the empty
partition $\varnothing$; $F_i$ adds and $E_i$ removes a node by the explicit
finite node formulas of the same item. The toral action is
$K_i|\lambda\rangle=q^{N_i(\lambda)}|\lambda\rangle$ with $N_i$ the
addable-minus-removable count, proved to be the Cartan pairing in
[[lem-the-node-count-is-the-level-one-cartan-pairing]], and
$K_d|\lambda\rangle=q^{-m_0(\lambda)}|\lambda\rangle$.

A partition is **$e$-regular** if each positive part occurs with multiplicity
$<e$, and **$e$-restricted** if $\lambda_r-\lambda_{r+1}<e$ for every $r\ge1$
(with $\lambda_{r}=0$ beyond the length). These operators are declared linear
endomorphisms here; the affine relations proved later establish the actual
module structure, so nothing about $F$ is silently assumed in this Definition.

Let $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted partition, so that
$\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}<p$ for all $i\ge1$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A node $(r,c)$ of
the Young diagram $[\mu]$ is an **$i$-node** if its residue
$$\operatorname{res}(r,c):=c-r\bmod p$$
equals $i\in\mathbb Z/p$; the $i$-nodes of $\mu$ are its addable and removable
nodes of residue $i$
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]).

**The reduced $i$-signature.** Fix $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and list the $i$-nodes
of $\mu$ as $A_1,\dots,A_n$ from top to bottom, that is, in increasing row
index and, for equal row index, in increasing column index. Form the word
$\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m=+$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m=-$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r<s$, $\sigma_r=-$,
$\sigma_s=+$ and $\sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{s-1}=0$, replace $\sigma_r$ and
$\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$. The
resulting **reduced $i$-signature** has the form $+\cdots+- \cdots-$ with the
zeros deleted, and the nodes attached to its signs are:

- the **normal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the removable nodes corresponding to
  the $-$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **good $i$-node** is the topmost (first listed) of the normal $i$-nodes;
- the **conormal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the addable nodes corresponding to
  the $+$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **cogood $i$-node** is the bottommost (last listed) of the conormal
  $i$-nodes.

Write $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ for the numbers of normal and
of conormal $i$-nodes of $\mu$; the good $i$-node exists exactly when
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and the cogood $i$-node exactly when
$\varphi_i(\mu)>0$. At most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node occur,
for each residue.

**Well-definedness.** Each reduction step deletes two nonzero entries, so any
sequence of steps terminates after at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ steps, and in
the resulting word no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$: otherwise, take two
nonzero entries that are consecutive among the nonzero entries of the current
word and are ordered $-$, $+$; all entries strictly between them are $0$ by
the choice, so the pair would still be reducible. Hence, after deleting the zero entries, a terminal word is
$+^a-^b$ for some $a,b\ge0$; cancelled positions remain in their original
places and need not form a contiguous block. The terminal word does not depend on the
order in which reducible pairs are chosen: two reducible pairs cannot overlap
partially, because an endpoint of one pair lying strictly inside the other
would be a nonzero entry in a position that the other pair requires to be
$0$, and pairs sharing exactly one endpoint would similarly place a nonzero
entry strictly inside the other pair; so any two reducible pairs are either
disjoint (and the corresponding steps commute) or equal, there are no
critical pairs, and the rewriting relation is locally confluent. Uniqueness follows
by induction on the number of nonzero entries. A terminal word admits no
step. Otherwise, two distinct first steps commute and reach a common word
after one further step each. All these successor words have fewer nonzero
entries, so the induction hypothesis identifies their terminal words. Thus
any two reduction sequences have the same terminal word; in it the first surviving $-$ and the last surviving
$+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature,
the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well
defined. The empty partition has the unique addable node $(1,1)$, of residue $0$,
and no removable nodes. Its $0$-signature is $(+)$ and its other signatures
are empty. Thus $\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=0$ for every $i$,
$\varphi_0(\varnothing)=1$, and $\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for $i\ne0$.
It has no good node and its cogood $0$-node is $(1,1)$.

**Convention warning.** The residue $c-r$ used here is the negative of
Brundan's $\ell$-residue $r-c$, and a removable node of $\mu$ is normal here
exactly when its transposed node is normal in Brundan's sense for the
transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the
signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two
conventions
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

derivations.claim: For every $a \ge 1$ the multiplicity of the part $a$ in $\lambda'$ equals $\lambda_a - \lambda_{a+1}$. Indeed the columns of $[\lambda]$ of height at least $a$ are exactly the first $\lambda_a$ columns, because column $j$ has height $\#\{r : \lambda_r \ge j\} \ge a$ if and only if $j \le \lambda_a$; hence the columns of height exactly $a$ number $\lambda_a - \lambda_{a+1}$, and these heights are precisely the parts of $\lambda'$ by [F1].

Transposition of nodes: $(r,c) \in [\lambda]$ if and only if $(c,r) \in [\lambda']$, so $(r,c) \mapsto (c,r)$ is a bijection from the nodes of $\lambda$ onto the nodes of $\lambda'$. It preserves addability and removability: deleting $(r,c)$ from $[\lambda]$ leaves the diagram of a partition $\mu$ if and only if deleting $(c,r)$ from $[\lambda']$ leaves the diagram of $\mu'$, and the same argument with diagrams enlarged by one node gives addability. It negates the residue, $\operatorname{res}(c,r) = r - c = -(c-r) = -\operatorname{res}(r,c)$ in $I = \mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}$.

Distinct corners of a partition have distinct contents. Let $x = (r,c) \ne y = (s,d)$ be addable or removable nodes with equal content $c - r = d - s$; by [F2] each is of the form $(a,\lambda_a)$ (removable) or $(a,\lambda_a+1)$ (addable, the new bottom row included via $\lambda_{k+1} = 0$). If $r=s$, two distinct corners must be the removable and addable endpoints of that row, whose contents differ by $1$, so they cannot have equal content. Interchange the nodes if needed to take $r<s$. If $x$ and $y$ are both removable with $r < s$, then $\lambda_r \ge \lambda_s$ while $\lambda_r - r = \lambda_s - s$ forces $\lambda_r - \lambda_s = r - s < 0$, a contradiction. If both are addable with $r < s$, then $\lambda_r \ge \lambda_s$ while equal contents force $\lambda_r - \lambda_s = r - s < 0$, again a contradiction. If $x$ is removable and $y$ addable with $r < s$, equal contents give $\lambda_r - \lambda_s = r + 1 - s$; for $s \ge r+2$ the right side is at most $-1$, so $\lambda_r < \lambda_s$, contradicting $\lambda_r \ge \lambda_s$, and for $s = r+1$ it gives $\lambda_r = \lambda_s$, which contradicts the addability of $(s,\lambda_s+1)$, that is $\lambda_{s-1} = \lambda_r > \lambda_s$ (here $s \ge 2$ because $r \ge 1$). If $x$ is addable with smaller row $r$ than the removable $y = (s,\lambda_s)$, then $\lambda_r \ge \lambda_s$ while $\lambda_r + 1 - r = \lambda_s - s$ forces $\lambda_s - \lambda_r = s + 1 - r \ge 2$, contradicting $\lambda_r \ge \lambda_s$. All possible pairs are covered, so equal contents force $x = y$.

Consequently $\lambda$ is $e$-restricted, i.e. $\lambda_a - \lambda_{a+1} < e$ for all $a$, if and only if the part $a$ occurs in $\lambda'$ fewer than $e$ times, i.e. $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular: step 1.1 identifies the two lists of integers compared with $e$. For $\lambda = \varnothing$, where $\lambda_a = 0$ for all $a$, both conditions are the empty family of inequalities and both hold; for $a > k$ one has $\lambda_a - \lambda_{a+1} = 0 < e$, so the restrictedness condition is finite, and $m_i(\varnothing) = 0$ for all $i$.

Step 1.2 also gives the weight bookkeeping: the transposition bijects the residue-$i$ nodes of $\lambda$ onto the residue-$(-i)$ nodes of $\lambda'$, so $m_i(\lambda) = m_{-i}(\lambda')$ for every $i$. Hence $\operatorname{wt}(|\lambda'\rangle) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_j m_j(\lambda')\alpha_j = \Lambda_0 - \sum_j m_{-j}(\lambda)\alpha_j = \tau(\operatorname{wt}(M_\lambda))$: applying the transposition of labels to the weight is the reflection $i \mapsto -i$ on the coefficients. In particular the relabelled basis vector $M_\lambda$ is a weight vector of weight $\operatorname{wt}(M_\lambda)$ for the transported toral action, since $K_h^{\mathrm{sym}} M_\lambda = J^{-1}K_{\tau h}^{\mathrm{QG}} J M_\lambda = q^{\langle \tau h, \operatorname{wt}(|\lambda'\rangle)\rangle} M_\lambda = q^{\langle h, \tau\, \operatorname{wt}(|\lambda'\rangle)\rangle} M_\lambda = q^{\langle h, \operatorname{wt}(M_\lambda)\rangle} M_\lambda$, using that $\tau$ preserves the pairing and exchanges $h_j$ with $h_{-j}$ ([[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]).

The transported operators act by node moves with reflected colors. For any partition $\mu$, the QG operator $E_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}}$ sends $|\mu\rangle$ to a linear combination of $|\mu \setminus \gamma\rangle$ over the removable nodes $\gamma$ of $\mu$ of residue $-i$, and $F_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}}$ sends $|\mu\rangle$ to a combination of $|\mu \cup \beta\rangle$ over the addable nodes $\beta$ of $\mu$ of residue $-i$ ([[def-level-one-partition-fock-space-and-node-residues]]); conjugating by $J$ and using step 1.2, $E_i^{\mathrm{sym}}$ sends $M_\lambda$ ($J M_\lambda = |\lambda'\rangle$) to the $J^{-1}$-images of the results of removing residue-$(-i)$ removable nodes of $\lambda'$, that is, to combinations of $M_{\lambda \setminus \gamma}$ over the removable nodes $\gamma$ of $\lambda$ of residue $i$, and likewise $F_i^{\mathrm{sym}}$ adds residue-$i$ nodes of $\lambda$. Thus at the level of nodes the symmetric-group model uses the same residue labels as the modular signature of the Definition, not their negatives.

At quantum characteristic $e = 0$ the colors form the set $I = \mathbb{Z}$ and, by [F2] and step 1.3, each residue class contains at most one node of $\lambda$: an $i$-node is a corner of content exactly $i$, and there is at most one such corner. Hence the residue word of every color has length at most one, no cancellation can occur, and for every nonempty $\lambda$ the removable corner $(k,\lambda_k)$ of its last row is the good node of its own residue, so repeated good deletions carry $\lambda$ to $\varnothing$; consult the $e = 0$ case of the survey's level-one example, under which every level-one partition is a crystal label. No finite affine datum, charge or weight formula is asserted here.

The conjugation $C(\lambda) = \lambda'$ is a bijection from the $e$-restricted partition class onto the $e$-regular class by step 2.1, and it is not an involution of the $e$-restricted class: at $e = 3$ it sends the restricted shape $(1,1,1)$ to the non-restricted shape $(3)$, and at $e = 2$ it sends the restricted shape $(1,1,1,1)$ to the non-restricted shape $(4)$; the same-model sign (Mullineux) involution of the survey instead preserves the restricted label set and is computed by negating the residues of a good-node path inside it. In the group regime the published dictionary for conjugate-sign duality of simple labels is exactly the stated identification $D(\lambda) \cong D^{\lambda'} \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$ ([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]).

boundaries.evidence: The empty partition is handled in step 2.1: all lambda_a = 0 give the empty family of inequalities, so the empty partition is both e-restricted and e-regular, m_i(empty) = 0, and J fixes M_empty.
Charge 0 is an ordinary index of the root lattice and step 2.4 records the separate source convention for quantum characteristic e = 0; no zero denominator or zero-quantity convention is hidden.
The vacuum's single addable node (1,1) and the level-1 weights Lambda_i are covered by step 2.3, and the hypothesis e >= 2 excludes e = 1 where residues would coincide.

The standing finite hypothesis includes e=2; transposition still negates residues and exchanges the regular/restricted conditions. The equal-content proof in step 1.3 also includes distinct endpoints in one row.
The Definition fixes the first surviving minus and last surviving plus in the modular reading; it now explicitly reverses the node list in the comparison with the opposite cancellation convention.
J is an explicit basis relabelling and every transported operator is defined by a conjugation formula; steps 1.1-1.3 make no selection from a family of sets.
Step 2.1 proves the forward direction: lambda e-restricted implies lambda-prime e-regular, through the column-multiplicity identity of step 1.1.
Step 2.1 proves the converse direction by the same identity read the other way, and step 3.1 uses the full equivalence.

classes are exchanged by conjugation: $\lambda$ is $e$-restricted if and only if

increasing column index, obtaining $A_1,\dots,A_n$, and form the word
$\sigma = (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m = +$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m = -$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r < s$ with $\sigma_r = -$,
$\sigma_s = +$ and $\sigma_{r+1} = \dots = \sigma_{s-1} = 0$, replace
$\sigma_r,\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies above a $+$. The survivors
are the *normal* removable and *conormal* addable $i$-nodes; write
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda)$ and $\varphi_i(\lambda)$ for their numbers. If
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *good* $i$-node is the removable node
belonging to the first surviving $-$, and $\tilde e_i\lambda := \lambda$ with
that node deleted; if $\varphi_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *cogood* $i$-node is the
addable node belonging to the last surviving $+$, and $\tilde f_i\lambda$ is
$\lambda$ with that node added (otherwise the respective partial operator is
undefined). This is Kleshchev's reduced $i$-signature at charge $0$ and level

$$F_{\mathrm{QG}} = \bigoplus_{\lambda} \mathbb{Q}(q)\,|\lambda\rangle$$
be the charge-$0$ level-one partition Fock space with
$\operatorname{wt}(|\lambda\rangle) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$,
where $m_i(\lambda)$ is the number of nodes of $[\lambda]$ of residue $i$, and
with the declared finite node operators $F_i$, $E_i$, $K_h$, $K_d$ of
[[def-level-one-partition-fock-space-and-node-residues]] (the operators act on
*all* partitions). When the wedge bar $\psi$ is supplied by the global-basis
construction, transport it by the formula below; this convention does not
construct that bar. The **symmetric-group model** $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$
is the same $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-vector space with the basis relabelled
$M_\lambda := |\lambda'\rangle$; equivalently, $J : F_{\mathrm{sym}} \to F_{\mathrm{QG}}$

$$J M_\lambda = |\lambda'\rangle \qquad (\lambda \text{ a partition}),$$

**Partitions.** Let $n\ge 0$ be an integer. A **partition of $n$** is a finite
weakly decreasing sequence $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ of positive
integers with $\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_k=n$. Its entries are the **parts** of
$\lambda$ and $k$ is the **number of parts**. For $n=0$ the only partition is
the **empty partition** $\varnothing$, the empty sequence with $k=0$; for
$n\ge 1$ one has $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_k\ge 1$ and
$k\le n$. We write $\lambda\vdash n$. Trailing zeros are not parts: a finite
sequence of nonnegative integers ending in $0$ is not a partition, so the
number of parts of $\lambda$ is determined by $\lambda$ and
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ is a different data type from
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k,0)$.

**English Young diagrams.** The **(English) Young diagram** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$[\lambda]:=\{\,(i,j)\;:\;1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le \lambda_i\,\}\subseteq\mathbb N\times\mathbb N,$$
where $i$ numbers the **rows** downward and $j$ numbers the **columns**
rightward. An element of $[\lambda]$ is a **node**, or box, of the diagram. Row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ carries $\lambda_i$ nodes, and column $j$ carries
$$\lambda'_j:=\#\{\,i: \lambda_i\ge j\,\}$$
nodes, a quantity that is $0$ beyond the last column (and for every $j\ge1$ when $\lambda=\varnothing$). Since a partition is weakly
decreasing, $[\lambda]$ determines $\lambda$: if $[\mu]=[\lambda]$, then row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ is row $i$ of $[\mu]$, so $\mu_i=\lambda_i$ for every $i$
and $\mu=\lambda$. In particular $[\varnothing]=\emptyset$, the empty diagram.

**Conjugation.** The **conjugate partition** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$\lambda':=(\lambda'_1,\lambda'_2,\dots,\lambda'_{\lambda_1}),$$
the sequence of column heights of $[\lambda]$, with $\varnothing':=\varnothing$
for the empty partition. This is again a partition of $n$, and
$[\lambda']$ is the transpose of $[\lambda]$:
for $1\le i\le\lambda_1$ and $1\le j\le k$,
$$(i,j)\in[\lambda']\iff j\le\lambda'_i\iff \lambda_j\ge i\iff (j,i)\in[\lambda].$$
Outside these bounds neither diagram contains the corresponding node; for the empty partition both diagrams are empty.
Conjugation is an involution, $\lambda''=\lambda$, because
$\lambda''_i=\#\{j:\lambda'_j\ge i\}$ counts the columns of $[\lambda]$ of
height at least $i$, that is, the columns $j$ with at least $i$ rows of length
$\ge j$, which by weak decrease is exactly the set of $j\le\lambda_i$. Thus
$\lambda\mapsto\lambda'$ is a bijection on the partitions of $n$, exchanging
the number of parts with the largest part for nonempty partitions.

**Size zero.** The symmetric group of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is
$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]) for every
$n\ge 0$, and we fix

the trivial group; for $n=0$ the set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is empty and the group
acts trivially on every size-zero object below. This is the convention used
whenever the constructions of this page are read at $n=0$.

Fix a residue $i$ and a partition $\lambda$, and write the **signature** of
$\lambda$ at $i$ as the word in the symbols $+$ (addable $i$-node) and $-$
(removable $i$-node) whose letters are the addable and removable $i$-nodes of
$\lambda$ read in the fixed increasing-content order of
[[def-the-node-order-and-n-i-exponents-for-fock-space]]. Reduce the word by
cancelling adjacent pairs $-+$ as long as such a pair remains. The surviving
minus letters are called **normal removable** $i$-nodes, and the first surviving
minus is the **good node** of $\lambda$ for $e_i$; the surviving plus letters
are called **conormal addable** $i$-nodes, and the last surviving plus is the
**cogood node** for $f_i$. If no sign of the required type survives, the
corresponding operator is $0$ on $|\lambda\rangle$. Equivalently, reading the
signature in decreasing content with the same addable/removable symbols, one cancels $+-$
and takes the good node as the last surviving $-$ and the cogood node as the
first surviving $+$.

derivations.claim: We prove the order claim by a case distinction on the two types. Let $x = (r,c)$, $y = (s,d)$ be corners of the same residue with $r < s$. Case both removable: $c = \lambda_r$, $d = \lambda_s$ and $\lambda_r \ge \lambda_s$; if $\lambda_r = \lambda_s$ then $\lambda_{r+1} \ge \lambda_s = \lambda_r$ (weak decrease, and $r+1 \le s$), contradicting $\lambda_r > \lambda_{r+1}$ from [F1], so $c = \lambda_r > \lambda_s = d$. Case both addable: $c = \lambda_r+1$, $d = \lambda_s+1$, and if $\lambda_r = \lambda_s$ then $\lambda_{s-1} = \lambda_r = \lambda_s$ (as $r \le s-1$, weak decrease gives $\lambda_{s-1} \le \lambda_r$, while $\lambda_{s-1} \ge \lambda_s$), contradicting the addability condition $\lambda_{s-1} > \lambda_s$ of [F1]; hence $c = \lambda_r+1 > \lambda_s+1 = d$. Case $x$ removable and $y$ addable: $c = \lambda_r$ and $d = \lambda_s+1$; addability of $y$ gives $\lambda_{s-1} > \lambda_s$. If $s \ge r+2$, then $\lambda_r \ge \lambda_{s-1} \ge \lambda_s+1 = d$; equality $\lambda_r = d$ would force $\lambda_{r+1} \ge \lambda_{s-1} \ge d = \lambda_r$ (as $r+1 \le s-1$), contradicting removability $\lambda_r > \lambda_{r+1}$, so $c = \lambda_r > d$. If $s = r+1$, then $\lambda_r = \lambda_{s-1} > \lambda_s = d-1$, so $\lambda_r \ge d$; equality $\lambda_r = d$ would give $\operatorname{cont}(x) - \operatorname{cont}(y) = (c-d) + (s-r) = 1$, and equal residues would force $e \mid 1$, impossible for $e \ge 2$; hence $c > d$ in this case too. Case $x$ addable and $y$ removable: $c = \lambda_r+1$ and $d = \lambda_s \le \lambda_r$, so $c > d$. In every case $c > d$, and then $\operatorname{cont}(x) - \operatorname{cont}(y) = (c-d) + (s-r) > 0$: both the column index and the content strictly decrease along increasing row index.

The reduction of [F2] is independent of the order of its replacements. Call a pair $(j,i)$ with $j<i$ a valid pair of a word $w \in \{-,0,+\}^n$ if $w_j = -$, $w_i = +$ and all entries strictly between are $0$, and reduce $w$ greedily by scanning left to right, pushing each encountered $-$ and, at each $+$, cancelling it with the most recently pushed uncancelled $-$ if there is one, leaving the $+$ as a survivor otherwise; the scan is deterministic. If $(j,i)$ is a valid pair, then the scan of $w$ cancels the $+$ at $i$ with the $-$ at $j$: no entry strictly between $j$ and $i$ is nonzero, so at time $i$ the position $j$ is still uncancelled and is the most recent uncancelled $-$. Consequently passing from $w$ to the word $w^{\mathrm{c}}$ that is $w$ with positions $j,i$ set to $0$ yields the same scan pairing on all remaining positions: the stack contents before $j$ and after $i$ agree, and no decision is taken at $j$ or $i$ in $w^{\mathrm{c}}$. By induction on the number of replacements, every word reachable from $w$ by replacements has the same scan survivors as $w$, so every maximal reduction ends in the scan reduced word and that word is unique; in particular $\varepsilon$, $\varphi$ and the surviving nodes of [F2] are well defined.

Two distinct $i$-nodes of $\lambda$ share neither a row nor a column. Same row: the only corners in a row $r$ are the removable node $(r,\lambda_r)$ and, when it is addable, the node $(r,\lambda_r+1)$, whose columns differ by $1$; equal residues would force $e \mid 1$, impossible for $e \ge 2$, and a node is not repeated. Same column $d$: if both nodes are removable, $(r,\lambda_r)$ and $(s,\lambda_s)$ with $\lambda_r = \lambda_s = d$ and $r < s$, then $\lambda_{r+1} \ge \lambda_s = \lambda_r$ contradicts $\lambda_r > \lambda_{r+1}$; if both are addable, $(r,\lambda_r+1)$ and $(s,\lambda_s+1)$ with $\lambda_r = \lambda_s = d-1$ and $r < s$, then $\lambda_{s-1} \le \lambda_r = \lambda_s$ and $\lambda_{s-1} \ge \lambda_s$ give $\lambda_{s-1} = \lambda_s$, contradicting addability at row $s$; if $(r,\lambda_r)$ is removable and $(s,\lambda_s+1)$ addable with $\lambda_r = \lambda_s+1$ and $r < s$, then removability gives $\lambda_{r+1} \le \lambda_s$, while $s \ge r+2$ would give $\lambda_{r+1} \ge \lambda_{s-1} > \lambda_s$, that is $\lambda_{r+1} \ge \lambda_s+1$, a contradiction; hence $s = r+1$, and then the two contents differ by exactly $1$, because $\operatorname{cont}(s,\lambda_s+1) = \lambda_s+1-s = \lambda_r-(r+1) = \operatorname{cont}(r,\lambda_r)-1$, so equal residues would again force $e \mid 1$, impossible; finally the opposite mixed orientation is impossible because addability of $(r,d)$ would give $\lambda_r = d-1 < d = \lambda_s \le \lambda_r$ for $r<s$.

Conjugation reverses the reading order and preserves the signs. By [F4] transposition sends the $i$-nodes of $\lambda$ bijectively onto the $(-i)$-nodes of $\lambda'$, preserving addable/removable type, and negates contents. If $x_1,\dots,x_n$ is the top-to-bottom $i$-node list of $\lambda$, then by step 1.1 the contents $\operatorname{cont}(x_m)$ strictly decrease in $m$, so the contents of the images $x_m'$ strictly increase in $m$; by step 1.1 applied to $\lambda'$, increasing content is exactly bottom to top on the $\lambda'$ corner list. Hence $x_1',\dots,x_n'$ is the bottom-to-top $(-i)$-node list of $\lambda'$, and its sign word equals the sign word of $x_1,\dots,x_n$ because transposition preserves the type of every node.

By step 2.2 the two words being reduced are identical: the modular signature of $\lambda$ at residue $i$ lists $x_1,\dots,x_n$ top to bottom, and the reference order of [F3] applied to $\lambda'$ at residue $-i$ lists $x_1',\dots,x_n'$ by increasing content, which is the same sequence of signs. Both rules cancel $-+$ and select the first surviving $-$ as good and the last surviving $+$ as cogood, so their survivor patterns coincide position by position, and the selected node of $\lambda$ is the transposed node of the selected node of $\lambda'$: the good (removable) $i$-node of $\lambda$ transposes to the first-surviving-$-$, hence good, removable $(-i)$-node of $\lambda'$, and the cogood (addable) $i$-node transposes to the last-surviving-$+$, hence cogood, addable $(-i)$-node of $\lambda'$. The survivor counts also agree, $\varepsilon_i(\lambda) = \varepsilon_{-i}(\lambda')$ and $\varphi_i(\lambda) = \varphi_{-i}(\lambda')$ in the two readings.

Reversing a word exchanges the two descriptions. Cancelling a $-+$ pair of a word $w$ amounts to cancelling the corresponding $+-$ pair of the reversed word $w^{\mathrm{R}}$; the first surviving $-$ of $w$ is the last surviving $-$ of $w^{\mathrm{R}}$, and the last surviving $+$ of $w$ is the first surviving $+$ of $w^{\mathrm{R}}$. Applying this to the increasing-content $(-i)$-signature of $\lambda'$ rewrites the dictionary of step 3.1 in the decreasing-content form: cancel $+-$, delete at the last surviving $-$ and add at the first surviving $+$. Both forms describe one and the same reduction and select the same actual nodes of $\lambda'$, and by step 3.1 the same nodes of $\lambda$ after transposition.

No hypothesis on $\lambda$ beyond the corner combinatorics was used: steps 1.1 and 2.1 hold for every partition, and steps 1.2-4.1 are computations on the resulting sign words. The modular and reference readings therefore agree as signature computations on all partitions, and only the later restriction of the two models to their basic label sets selects a connected component from them.

boundaries.evidence: The empty partition has one addable corner (1,1), of residue 0, and no removable corner. Its residue-0 word is + and its other words are empty; the dictionary preserves these words.
Zeros are the cancelled positions of a +-word; step 1.2's scan skips them and step 4.1 reverses them without change.
A length-one word is its own reduction: step 1.2's scan keeps a single sign and step 4.1's reversal acts trivially.
At e = 2 the only way two same-residue corners share a column is the adjacent-row mixed configuration, and step 2.1 isolates and excludes exactly that case via e | 1.
The first surviving - and the last surviving + are the endpoints of the reduced word, and steps 3.1 and 4.1 track them through conjugation and reversal.
Every selection in steps 1.1-1.2 is forced by the row order and the deterministic reduction; no choice function occurs.

boundaries.reason: The lemma proves an order and selection dictionary rather than a biconditional claim, so there is no forward direction of an equivalence to discharge; the one implication it does state, smaller row implies larger column, is proved in step 1.1.
No converse of the row-order implication is asserted, and the dictionary of step 3.1 is an identity of two reduction procedures rather than a two-way implication.

Cartan datum, its lattices and its diagram reflection $\tau$ fixed as in
[[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]: $I = \mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}$, simple
roots $\alpha_i$, fundamental weights $\Lambda_i$, $\delta$, and
$\tau(i) = -i$. A *node* is a pair $(r,c) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, and
the *residue* of a node is $\operatorname{res}(r,c) := c - r \bmod e$; this is
the level-one, charge-$0$ specialization of the residue used in
[[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]. We use the
English convention (rows increase downwards) and the node language of
[[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]] and
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]].

A partition $\lambda$ is **$e$-regular** if every positive integer occurs as a
part of $\lambda$ fewer than $e$ times, and **$e$-restricted** if
$\lambda_a - \lambda_{a+1} < e$ for every $a \ge 1$, the sequence being padded
by trailing zeros; these are the prime-case notions of
[[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]] with $e$ in place of the prime
$p$. A column of height $e$ is allowed in an $e$-restricted partition. The two
classes are exchanged by conjugation: $\lambda$ is $e$-restricted if and only if
its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular (step 2.1 below).

**The modular (restricted) signature.** Let $\lambda$ be a partition and
$i \in I$. The $i$-nodes of $\lambda$ are its addable and removable nodes of
residue $i$; list them *top to bottom*, that is by increasing row index and then
increasing column index, obtaining $A_1,\dots,A_n$, and form the word
$\sigma = (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m = +$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m = -$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r < s$ with $\sigma_r = -$,
$\sigma_s = +$ and $\sigma_{r+1} = \dots = \sigma_{s-1} = 0$, replace
$\sigma_r,\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies above a $+$. The survivors
are the *normal* removable and *conormal* addable $i$-nodes; write
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda)$ and $\varphi_i(\lambda)$ for their numbers. If
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *good* $i$-node is the removable node
belonging to the first surviving $-$, and $\tilde e_i\lambda := \lambda$ with
that node deleted; if $\varphi_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *cogood* $i$-node is the
addable node belonging to the last surviving $+$, and $\tilde f_i\lambda$ is
$\lambda$ with that node added (otherwise the respective partial operator is
undefined). This is Kleshchev's reduced $i$-signature at charge $0$ and level
one, with good $=$ top normal and cogood $=$ bottom conormal. **This is the
reading used for the restricted (symmetric-group) model**, in which the labels
of the level-one basic module are the $e$-restricted shapes; Fayers' equivalent
formulation reads the list in reverse order, with the opposite cancellation, and extracts the
last surviving $- $ and first surviving $+$, and his increasing-column model of
the $e$-restricted labels is the basic crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$.

$$F_{\mathrm{QG}} = \bigoplus_{\lambda} \mathbb{Q}(q)\,|\lambda\rangle$$
be the charge-$0$ level-one partition Fock space with
$\operatorname{wt}(|\lambda\rangle) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$,
where $m_i(\lambda)$ is the number of nodes of $[\lambda]$ of residue $i$, and
with the declared finite node operators $F_i$, $E_i$, $K_h$, $K_d$ of
[[def-level-one-partition-fock-space-and-node-residues]] (the operators act on
*all* partitions). When the wedge bar $\psi$ is supplied by the global-basis
construction, transport it by the formula below; this convention does not
construct that bar. The **symmetric-group model** $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$
is the same $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-vector space with the basis relabelled
$M_\lambda := |\lambda'\rangle$; equivalently, $J : F_{\mathrm{sym}} \to F_{\mathrm{QG}}$
is the $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-linear isomorphism
$$J M_\lambda = |\lambda'\rangle \qquad (\lambda \text{ a partition}),$$
with the field map $q \mapsto q$ (not $q \mapsto q^{-1}$). Transport the
structure along $J$:
$$E_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} E_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad F_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} F_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad K_h^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} K_{\tau h}^{\mathrm{QG}} J \quad (h \in P^\vee), \qquad \psi_{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} \psi J,$$

$\operatorname{wt}(M_\lambda) := \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$. The
transported operators are defined on the ambient basis of *all* partitions.

$A_0 := \{\, f \in \mathbb{Q}(q) : f \text{ is regular at } q = 0 \,\}$, the
**standard chart** of the symmetric-group model is
$$(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}} := \bigoplus_{\lambda} A_0\, M_\lambda ;$$
the full ambient model is indexed by all partitions, while its basic component
in this convention is carried by the $e$-restricted shapes (the comparison with
the QG model is made by the results of this page).

addable/removable *type* of each node and negates residues; it is a comparison
map *between* the restricted and the regular models, not an involution of one
label set, and it is not the same-model sign (Mullineux) involution of

dual-Specht convention and the $e$-regular partitions those of James, the two
dictionaries being related by

([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]);

characteristic (the smallest positive $e$ with $1 + \xi + \dots + \xi^{e-1} = 0$)

where $B$ is the cogood $i$-node of $\mu$, the operator being undefined on

index and, for equal row index, in increasing column index. Form the word

resulting **reduced $i$-signature** has the form $+\cdots+- \cdots-$ with the
zeros deleted, and the nodes attached to its signs are:

- the **normal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the removable nodes corresponding to
  the $-$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **good $i$-node** is the topmost (first listed) of the normal $i$-nodes;
- the **conormal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the addable nodes corresponding to
  the $+$ signs of the reduced signature;

$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and the cogood $i$-node exactly when
$\varphi_i(\mu)>0$. At most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node occur,
for each residue.

**Well-definedness.** Each reduction step deletes two nonzero entries, so any
sequence of steps terminates after at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ steps, and in
the resulting word no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$: otherwise, take two
nonzero entries that are consecutive among the nonzero entries of the current
word and are ordered $-$, $+$; all entries strictly between them are $0$ by
the choice, so the pair would still be reducible. Hence, after deleting the zero entries, a terminal word is
$+^a-^b$ for some $a,b\ge0$; cancelled positions remain in their original
places and need not form a contiguous block. The terminal word does not depend on the
order in which reducible pairs are chosen: two reducible pairs cannot overlap
partially, because an endpoint of one pair lying strictly inside the other
would be a nonzero entry in a position that the other pair requires to be
$0$, and pairs sharing exactly one endpoint would similarly place a nonzero
entry strictly inside the other pair; so any two reducible pairs are either
disjoint (and the corresponding steps commute) or equal, there are no
critical pairs, and the rewriting relation is locally confluent. Uniqueness follows
by induction on the number of nonzero entries. A terminal word admits no
step. Otherwise, two distinct first steps commute and reach a common word
after one further step each. All these successor words have fewer nonzero
entries, so the induction hypothesis identifies their terminal words. Thus
any two reduction sequences have the same terminal word; in it the first surviving $-$ and the last surviving
$+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature,
the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well
defined. The empty partition has the unique addable node $(1,1)$, of residue $0$,
and no removable nodes. Its $0$-signature is $(+)$ and its other signatures
are empty. Thus $\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=0$ for every $i$,
$\varphi_0(\varnothing)=1$, and $\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for $i\ne0$.

Brundan's $\ell$-residue $r-c$, and a removable node of $\mu$ is normal here
exactly when its transposed node is normal in Brundan's sense for the
transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the
signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two
conventions

[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

signature in decreasing content with the same addable/removable symbols, one cancels $+-$

first surviving $+$.

$B_F=\{|\lambda\rangle+qF_0:\lambda\text{ a partition}\}$. The normalized
Kashiwara operators remove the good normal $i$-node and add the cogood conormal
$i$-node of the corrected signature of
[[def-good-and-cogood-nodes-by-residue-signature-reduction]], and
$\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i$ are the surviving minus/plus counts. The graph is a
graph on all partitions, not only regular ones; its empty connected component
is precisely the set of $e$-regular partitions, while the $e$-restricted labels
belong to the transposed model. A pole or a unique Chevalley term does not
determine a crystal arrow.

derivations.claim: For every partition $\mu$ and every color $i$, the selection operations of the two readings correspond under transposition. By [F2] the top-to-bottom $i$-node word of $\mu$ equals the increasing-content $(-i)$-node word of $\mu'$ position by position, with the same signs, so the reduced survivor words coincide; consequently $\varepsilon_i(\mu) = \varepsilon_{-i}(\mu')$ and $\varphi_i(\mu) = \varphi_{-i}(\mu')$, and if $\varepsilon_i(\mu) > 0$ then the good $i$-node of $\mu$ is the transposed node of the good $(-i)$-node of $\mu'$, while if $\varphi_i(\mu) > 0$ then the cogood $i$-node of $\mu$ is the transposed node of the cogood $(-i)$-node of $\mu'$. In particular $\varepsilon_i(\mu) = 0$ if and only if $\varepsilon_{-i}(\mu') = 0$.

There is no naming-polarity swap between the two conventions: in the modular reading the good node is by definition removable and the cogood node addable ([F1]), in the $p$-restricted operator definition the good node is removable and the cogood node addable ([F3]), and in the Fock-space reading the good node is the surviving $-$, hence removable, while the cogood node is the surviving $+$, hence addable ([F4]); the normalized Fock operators remove the good node and add the cogood node ([F5]). Hence both dictionaries compare a deletion with a deletion and an addition with an addition, and the only change is the color reflection $i \mapsto -i$.

The transported crystal operators on all partition residues are given by the modular signature rule. The field operators $J^{-1}\tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}J$ and $J^{-1}\tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}J$ preserve $(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}}$ by [F5]; let $b_\mu:=M_\mu+q(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}}$. The induced map of residue spaces sends $b_\mu$ to $|\mu'\rangle+qF_0$. By [F4]-[F5] its raising image is the residue of the partition obtained by deleting the good $(-i)$-node of $\mu'$, or zero when no such node exists. Step 1.1 identifies that node with the transpose of the modular good $i$-node $A$ of $\mu$, so $\tilde e_i^{\mathrm{sym}}b_\mu=b_{\mu\setminus A}$ when $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and zero otherwise. The same argument gives $\tilde f_i^{\mathrm{sym}}b_\mu=b_{\mu\cup B}$ for the modular cogood node $B$, and zero when $\varphi_i(\mu)=0$. These are equalities of crystal residues: on raw standard vectors they assert congruences modulo $q(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}}$, including at zero arrows, rather than exact field-vector equalities.

Weights transform by the reflection. By [F1] the transported weight satisfies $\operatorname{wt}(M_\mu) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\mu)\alpha_i$ and $m_i(\mu) = m_{-i}(\mu')$; hence $\operatorname{wt}(|\mu'\rangle) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_j m_j(\mu')\alpha_j = \Lambda_0 - \sum_j m_{-j}(\mu)\alpha_j = \tau(\operatorname{wt}(M_\mu))$, and the weight of a crystal arrow is preserved by the node moves of step 2.1 because those moves change one residue count by one on each side consistently.

Restricted case. Let $\lambda$ be $e$-restricted, so that $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular by [F1] and hence a vertex of the empty component of the full Fock crystal by [F5], on which the operators $\tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}$, $\tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}$ of [F5] act. By step 2.1 applied at $\mu = \lambda$, the modular operator $\tilde e_i$ on $\lambda$ (delete the good $i$-node, zero if $\varepsilon_i(\lambda) = 0$) is intertwined with $\tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}$ on $\lambda'$: $C\,\tilde e_i\lambda = \tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}C\lambda$, and likewise $C\,\tilde f_i\lambda = \tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}C\lambda$, both sides being zero together by the count agreement of step 1.1. Since transposition is a bijection from the $e$-restricted onto the $e$-regular labels and [F5] identifies the latter precisely as the vertex set of the empty component, the conjugation of the modular restricted graph is exactly that empty component, with colors negated; for $e = p$ prime the modular side is the operator system of [F3], and in general it is the reading fixed in [F1].

Finally, the arrows are not read off from ordinary Chevalley coefficients. The selection is the signature reduction of [F4], and [F4]-[F5] record that a pole or a unique Chevalley term does not determine the crystal arrow; the transported operator $\tilde e^{\mathrm{sym}}_i$ of step 2.1 is the normalization inherited from $\tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}$, not the transported Chevalley operator $E_i^{\mathrm{sym}} = J^{-1}E_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}}J$, whose coefficients (such as $q^{-1}$ from the formulas of Leclerc (38)-(39)) differ from the arrow data.

Zero values are covered by the count agreement of step 1.1: epsilon_i(mu) = 0 exactly when epsilon_{-i}(mu-prime) = 0, so both sides of the arrow identity vanish together.
Single surviving signs are selected by the first- and last-surviving rules, whose coincidence under conjugation is the position-by-position identification of step 2.1.
At e = 2 the color reflection is the identity on Z/2, so the dictionary reduces to step 1.2's color-fixed comparison without a separate case.
Step 2.1 tracks the selected endpoints as crystal residues. It asserts only congruences on raw vectors modulo q times the transported chart, including when the crystal arrow is zero.
No choice occurs: step 2.1 reconstructs the transported normalized operators from the explicit conjugation by J, and the selections are deterministic.
One direction of the stated zero equivalence is step 1.1's count identity: epsilon_i(mu) = 0 forces epsilon_{-i}(mu-prime) = 0.
The converse direction is step 1.1 read in the other direction, since the count identity is symmetric between mu and mu-prime.
