with the field map $q \mapsto q$ (not $q \mapsto q^{-1}$). Transport the
structure along $J$:
$$E_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} E_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad F_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} F_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad K_h^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} K_{\tau h}^{\mathrm{QG}} J \quad (h \in P^\vee), \qquad \psi_{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} \psi J,$$
and give $M_\lambda$ the weight
$\operatorname{wt}(M_\lambda) := \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$. The
transported operators are defined on the ambient basis of *all* partitions.
With $A := \mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$ and the local ring
$A_0 := \{\, f \in \mathbb{Q}(q) : f \text{ is regular at } q = 0 \,\}$, the
**standard chart** of the symmetric-group model is
$$(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}} := \bigoplus_{\lambda} A_0\, M_\lambda ;$$
the full ambient model is indexed by all partitions, while its basic component
in this convention is carried by the $e$-restricted shapes (the comparison with
the QG model is made by the results of this page).

**Label dictionaries and boundaries.** The conjugation map $C : \lambda \mapsto \lambda'$
exchanges the $e$-restricted and the $e$-regular partitions, preserves the
addable/removable *type* of each node and negates residues; it is a comparison
map *between* the restricted and the regular models, not an involution of one
label set, and it is not the same-model sign (Mullineux) involution of
Kleshchev's Theorem 11.8, which fixes the restricted label set and negates
residues along a good-node path. In the symmetric-group regime (ground field of
characteristic $p > 0$, Hecke parameter $\xi = 1$, so that $e = p$ is prime) the
$e$-restricted partitions are the labels of the simple modules in the
dual-Specht convention and the $e$-regular partitions those of James, the two
dictionaries being related by
$D(\lambda) \cong D^{\lambda'} \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$, equivalently
$D^\mu \cong D(\mu') \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$ for $e$-regular $\mu$
([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]);
for a general Hecke parameter the finite integer $e \ge 2$ is its quantum
characteristic (the smallest positive $e$ with $1 + \xi + \dots + \xi^{e-1} = 0$)
and need not be prime, so the general finite-$e$ crystal labels are not called
symmetric-group modules of "characteristic $e$". At quantum characteristic
$e = 0$ (no such positive integer exists, colors $\mathbb{Z}$) no finite affine
datum is present: every level-one partition is a crystal label, and no weight
formula or finite affine statement is made in this boundary.

Consider the modular reading on the one hand (the top-to-bottom residue
signature with good $=$ first surviving $-$ and cogood $=$ last surviving $+$ of
[[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]], whose
operators delete the good node and add the cogood node on $e$-restricted
labels) and the level-one Fock crystal $\tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_i$,
$\tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}_i$ on the other. Conjugation
$C(\lambda) = \lambda'$ sends the modular operators on $e$-restricted
partitions onto the normalized operators of the **empty connected component** of
the QG full partition Fock crystal, with the colors negated:
$$C\,\tilde e_i\lambda = \tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}C\lambda, \qquad C\,\tilde f_i\lambda = \tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}C\lambda \qquad (\lambda\ e\text{-restricted}),$$
including the zero values: the left side is zero exactly when the right side is.
The survivor counts are the same on both sides,
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda) = \varepsilon_{-i}(\lambda')$ and
$\varphi_i(\lambda) = \varphi_{-i}(\lambda')$, and the weight transforms by the
diagram reflection, $\operatorname{wt}(\lambda') = \tau(\operatorname{wt}(\lambda))$.
With the transported full module $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$ of
[[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]], the
modular signatures likewise give its normalized operators on **all** partitions
(the transported operators $J^{-1}\tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}J$,
$J^{-1}\tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}J$), and the restricted subset of that full
crystal is its basic component. In both conventions good means removable
(deletion, $\tilde e$) and cogood means addable (addition, $\tilde f$): there is
no opposite naming-polarity dictionary exchanging deletion with addition.
Ordinary Chevalley coefficients, especially negative powers such as $q^{-1}$,
do not define these arrows.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

With the declared use of the Axiom of Choice in the general integrable-module
decomposition, the empty connected component of the full partition crystal of
[[thm-the-crystal-of-level-one-fock-space-is-the-good-node-partition-graph]] is
the canonical highest weight crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$, with exactly the
$e$-regular labels. Its module is $M=U_q(\mathfrak g)|\varnothing\rangle$ and
its lower $A_0$-lattice is $M\cap F_0$; it occurs once. More precisely

$$F=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}V(\Lambda_0-k\delta)^{\oplus p(k)},$$

a locally weight-finite indexed direct sum in which $p(k)$ is the number of
ordinary partitions of $k$; consequently
$\mathrm{ch}\,F=\mathrm{ch}\,V(\Lambda_0)\prod_{r\ge1}(1-e^{-r\delta})^{-1}$.
A highest **crystal** label need not be a highest **field** standard vector, and
the ambient canonical basis need not split these summands.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$. Every $p$-restricted partition
$\mu$ of $d$ is obtained from the empty partition by $d$ successive cogood
additions: there are residues $i_1,\dots,i_d$ with
$$\mu=\tilde f_{i_d}\cdots\tilde f_{i_1}\varnothing;$$
equivalently, every $p$-restricted $\mu\ne\varnothing$ has at least one good
node, and successive good deletions carry $\mu$ to $\varnothing$
([[def-good-node-and-cogood-node-crystal-operators]],
[[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). Hence, in
the graph whose vertices are the $p$-restricted partitions and whose edges
join $\nu$ to $\tilde f_i\nu$ for every $i$ for which the operator is
defined, the empty partition is the unique vertex of rank $0$ and every
vertex is reached from it; dually every vertex reaches the empty partition by
successive good deletions. The argument is choice-free.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $L_1,\dots,L_n\in kS_n$
be the Jucys-Murphy elements $L_r=\sum_{s<r}(s,r)$ of the symmetric group
algebra ([[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]). Recall
that they commute pairwise
([[cor-jucys-murphy-elements-commute-pairwise]]), and for $r\le n$ the
element $L_r$ lies in the subalgebra $kS_r\subseteq kS_n$ and therefore
commutes with $S_{r-1}$.

**(i) Primary idempotents.** In the commutative subalgebra
$k[L_1,\dots,L_n]\subseteq kS_n$ the minimal polynomial of each $L_r$ on the
regular module splits into linear factors $X-a$ with $a$ in the prime field
$\mathbb F_p\subseteq k$, and the commuting family admits the following
simultaneous primary decomposition. There are pairwise orthogonal idempotents
$P_{r,a}\in k[L_r]\subseteq k[L_1,\dots,L_n]$, indexed by $r\in\{1,\dots,n\}$
and $a\in\mathbb F_p$, with
$$\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p}P_{r,a}=1,\qquad P_{r,a}P_{r,b}=\delta_{a,b}P_{r,a},$$
such that for every finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module $M$ the action of
$P_{r,a}$ on $M$ is the projection onto the generalized eigenspace
$M_{r,a}=\{m\in M:(L_r-a)^Nm=0\text{ for }N\gg0\}$. The $P_{r,a}$ for
different $r$ commute, and for each sequence $\mathbf i=(i_1,\dots,i_n)$
with entries in $\mathbb F_p$ the products
$$e(\mathbf i):=\prod_{r=1}^nP_{r,i_r}\ \in\ k[L_1,\dots,L_n]$$
are pairwise orthogonal idempotents with $\sum_{\mathbf i}e(\mathbf i)=1$ and
$e(\mathbf i)M=M_{\mathbf i}$, the simultaneous generalized weight space
$M_{\mathbf i}=\{m:(L_r-i_r)^Nm=0\ \forall r,\ N\gg0\}$. Every $P_{r,a}$ and
every $e(\mathbf i)$ is fixed by the antipode $g\mapsto g^{-1}$ of $kS_n$.

**(ii) Content sums and blocks.** The symmetric group $S_n$ permutes the
coordinates of sequences, and two sequences are called *equivalent* when they
differ by a permutation, i.e. when they have the same content (the same
multiset of entries of $\mathbb F_p$). Write $\mathcal C_n=(\mathbb F_p)^n/S_n$ for the set of content classes
(equivalently, multisets of $n$ residues). For $\alpha\in\mathcal C_n$ let
$I_\alpha$ be the set of sequences representing $\alpha$, and put
$$e_\alpha:=\sum_{\mathbf i\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf i)\ \in\ kS_n .$$
Each $e_\alpha$ is a central idempotent of $kS_n$, and distinct $e_\alpha$
are orthogonal; the nonzero $e_\alpha$ are exactly the primitive central
idempotents, that is the block idempotents of $kS_n$
([[def-p-blocks-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]), and every block
idempotent of $kS_n$ is of the form $e_\alpha$: this last identification of
the content sums with the blocks is the block theorem of Lyle-Mathas and
Brundan recorded as (2.41) in Kleshchev's survey (printed p. 14), with the
content of the block being the content of any of its partitions. The present
item proves centrality, idempotency, orthogonality, primitivity and
exhaustiveness locally; the residue functors use the first three properties.

**(iii) Residue-summand functors.** For a finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module
$M$, a residue $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and a content class
$\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}$, put
$$e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}:=\sum_{\mathbf j\in I_\alpha}e((\mathbf j,i)) \ =\ e_\alpha^{(n-1)}\,P_{n,i},$$
where $(\mathbf j,i)$ denotes concatenation, $e_\alpha^{(n-1)}=\sum_{\mathbf
j\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf j)$ is the content sum computed in $kS_{n-1}$ and
regarded in $kS_n$ through the inclusion $kS_{n-1}\subseteq kS_n$, and
$P_{n,i}\in k[L_n]$. Each $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ is an idempotent of $kS_n$
commuting with $kS_{n-1}$, the family
$\{e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\}_{i\in\mathbb F_p,\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}}$ is a family of pairwise orthogonal
idempotents with $\sum_{i,\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=1$, and
$$E_iM:=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M =\bigoplus_{\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M$$
is a $kS_{n-1}$-submodule of the restricted module with
$$\operatorname{Res}^{S_n}_{S_{n-1}}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}E_iM .$$
Dually, for a finite-dimensional $kS_d$-module $M$ of content
$\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$, i.e. $M=e_\alpha^{(d)}M$, put
$$F_iM:=kS_{d+1}\,e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}M \qquad(i\in\mathbb Z/p),$$
with $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,i}\in kS_{d+1}$; for a
general finite-dimensional $M$, with the sum indexed by $\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$, put
$F_iM:=\bigoplus_\alpha kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M$.
Then $\operatorname{Ind}^{S_{d+1}}_{S_d}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}F_iM$,
and all the functors $E_i,F_i$ are additive and exact, preserve
finite-dimensionality, and commute with contragredient duality, because the
projectors are fixed by the antipode. All statements hold at $p=2$; the
construction is choice-free.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, $\mu$ a $p$-restricted partition
of $d$ and $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ with $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$; let $A$ be the good
$i$-node and $\nu=\mu\setminus A$
([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). For the
residue-summand functor $E_i$ of
[[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]] the
module $E_iD(\mu)$ has simple socle and simple head, both isomorphic to
$D(\nu)$, and the total (ungraded) multiplicity of $D(\nu)$ in $E_iD(\mu)$ is
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)$. Thus the Loewy endpoints are simple even though the
formal character of $E_iD(\mu)$ may contain the additional normal-node
factors of
[[thm-normal-node-composition-multiplicities-under-residue-restriction]].

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For $\mu\vdash n$
write $S^\mu_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\mu_{\mathbb Z}$ for the field-valued
Specht module, $D^\mu=S^\mu_k/R^\mu$ for its modular form quotient
([[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]]), and let
$$S(\mu):=(S^\mu_k)^*=\operatorname{Hom}_k(S^\mu_k,k),\qquad (\sigma\cdot f)(x):=f(\sigma^{-1}x)$$
be the **dual Specht module**, with
$$D(\mu):=\operatorname{hd}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr) =S(\mu)/\operatorname{rad}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr)$$
its head ([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]). Let
$\mu'$ be the conjugate partition, and let
$S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ be the tensor product of
$k[S_n]$-modules with the diagonal action
$\sigma\cdot(x\otimes w)=(\sigma\cdot x)\otimes(\sigma\cdot w)$, where
$\operatorname{sgn}$ is the one-dimensional sign representation
([[def-sign-representation-and-restriction-of-a-representation]],
[[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]).

1. **Dual Specht versus sign-twisted conjugate.** If $\mu$ is $p$-restricted
   (equivalently, by
   [[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]], $\mu'$ is $p$-regular),
   then $S(\mu)\cong S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$; consequently
   $S(\mu)$ is nonzero with simple head
   $$D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn},$$
   a nonzero simple $k[S_n]$-module that is self-dual and absolutely
   irreducible.
2. **Equivalent form for $p$-regular labels.** If $\lambda\vdash n$ is
   $p$-regular, then $\lambda'$ is $p$-restricted and
   $$D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')\otimes\operatorname{sgn}.$$
3. **The two labellings.** The map $\mu\mapsto D(\mu)$ is a bijection from
   the set of $p$-restricted partitions of $n$ to the set of isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; that is, every simple
   $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D(\mu)$ for exactly one $p$-restricted
   $\mu\vdash n$.

In characteristic $2$ the sign representation is the trivial representation,
so the formulas read $D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}$ and $D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')$;
the transposition is still required, and the two labellings coincide only
for self-conjugate partitions. No step divides by a group order or uses
averaging, and $n=0$ is included.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $R$ be a commutative ring. In the group ring $R[S_n]$ of
the symmetric group on $\{1,\dots,n\}$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-symmetric-group]], [[def-group-ring]]), where $(j\ k)$ denotes the
transposition of the distinct entries $j,k\in\{1,\dots,n\}$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), the **Jucys-Murphy elements** are
$$X_1:=0,\qquad X_k:=\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}(j\ k)\in R[S_n]\qquad(2\le k\le n).$$
Each $X_k$ is a finite sum of group elements with coefficient $1$, so the
formula already defines an element of the integral group ring
$\mathbb Z[S_n]$, and its image under the base change
$\mathbb Z[S_n]\to R[S_n]$ is the displayed element
([[def-restriction-and-extension-of-scalars]]); for $1\le k\le m\le n$ the element
$X_k$ of $R[S_m]$, computed in the subgroup
$S_m=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,m\})\subseteq S_n$ of permutations fixing
$m+1,\dots,n$, maps to $X_k$ under the inclusion $S_m\hookrightarrow S_n$.
Equivalently $X_k=T_k-T_{k-1}$, where $T_k=\sum_{1\le i<j\le k}(i\ j)$ is the
sum of all transpositions in $S_k$.

Let $k$ be a field.

For the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]), the **sign
representation** over $k$ is the one-dimensional representation on $k$ in which
$$\sigma \cdot a:=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)a.$$
This is a representation because $\operatorname{sgn}:S_n \to \{\pm 1\}$ is a
group homomorphism ([[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]).

Now let $\rho:G \to \operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a representation of a group $G$
over $k$, and let $H \le G$ be a subgroup ([[def-subgroup]]). The
**restriction** of $\rho$ to $H$ is the representation
$$\operatorname{Res}^G_H(V):=\rho|_H:H \longrightarrow \operatorname{GL}(V),\qquad h \longmapsto \rho(h).$$
It has the same underlying vector space $V$ and only forgets the action of the
elements outside $H$.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra and $M$ a finite-dimensional left
$A$-module.

- Its **radical** is
  $$   \operatorname{rad}(M)=J(A)M,   $$
  equivalently the intersection of the maximal submodules, by
  [[thm-module-radical-is-jacobson-radical-times-the-module]].

- Its **socle** $\operatorname{Soc}(M)$ is the sum of all simple submodules, as
  in [[def-socle-of-a-module]].

- Its **head** or **top** is the quotient
  $$   \operatorname{hd}(M):=M/\operatorname{rad}(M),   $$
  formed using [[def-quotient-module]].

- Its **Loewy series** is the descending radical filtration
  $$   M\supseteq \operatorname{rad}(M)\supseteq \operatorname{rad}^2(M)\supseteq\cdots   $$
  together with the corresponding semisimple layers
  $\operatorname{rad}^i(M)/\operatorname{rad}^{i+1}(M)$.

The simple subquotients appearing in the Loewy layers are simple in the sense
of [[def-simple-module]].

Fix a finite integer $e \ge 2$ and charge $0$, with the independent-root affine
Cartan datum, its lattices and its diagram reflection $\tau$ fixed as in
[[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]: $I = \mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}$, simple
roots $\alpha_i$, fundamental weights $\Lambda_i$, $\delta$, and
$\tau(i) = -i$. A *node* is a pair $(r,c) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, and
the *residue* of a node is $\operatorname{res}(r,c) := c - r \bmod e$; this is
the level-one, charge-$0$ specialization of the residue used in
[[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]. We use the
English convention (rows increase downwards) and the node language of
[[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]] and
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]].

A partition $\lambda$ is **$e$-regular** if every positive integer occurs as a
part of $\lambda$ fewer than $e$ times, and **$e$-restricted** if
$\lambda_a - \lambda_{a+1} < e$ for every $a \ge 1$, the sequence being padded
by trailing zeros; these are the prime-case notions of
[[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]] with $e$ in place of the prime
$p$. A column of height $e$ is allowed in an $e$-restricted partition. The two
classes are exchanged by conjugation: $\lambda$ is $e$-restricted if and only if
its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular (step 2.1 below).

**The modular (restricted) signature.** Let $\lambda$ be a partition and
$i \in I$. The $i$-nodes of $\lambda$ are its addable and removable nodes of
residue $i$; list them *top to bottom*, that is by increasing row index and then
increasing column index, obtaining $A_1,\dots,A_n$, and form the word
$\sigma = (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m = +$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m = -$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r < s$ with $\sigma_r = -$,
$\sigma_s = +$ and $\sigma_{r+1} = \dots = \sigma_{s-1} = 0$, replace
$\sigma_r,\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies above a $+$. The survivors
are the *normal* removable and *conormal* addable $i$-nodes; write
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda)$ and $\varphi_i(\lambda)$ for their numbers. If
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *good* $i$-node is the removable node
belonging to the first surviving $-$, and $\tilde e_i\lambda := \lambda$ with
that node deleted; if $\varphi_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *cogood* $i$-node is the
addable node belonging to the last surviving $+$, and $\tilde f_i\lambda$ is
$\lambda$ with that node added (otherwise the respective partial operator is
undefined). This is Kleshchev's reduced $i$-signature at charge $0$ and level
one, with good $=$ top normal and cogood $=$ bottom conormal. **This is the
reading used for the restricted (symmetric-group) model**, in which the labels
of the level-one basic module are the $e$-restricted shapes; Fayers' equivalent
formulation reads the list in reverse order, with the opposite cancellation, and extracts the
last surviving $- $ and first surviving $+$, and his increasing-column model of
the $e$-restricted labels is the basic crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$.

**The linear (symmetric-group) model and the transport $J$.** Let
$$F_{\mathrm{QG}} = \bigoplus_{\lambda} \mathbb{Q}(q)\,|\lambda\rangle$$
be the charge-$0$ level-one partition Fock space with
$\operatorname{wt}(|\lambda\rangle) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$,
where $m_i(\lambda)$ is the number of nodes of $[\lambda]$ of residue $i$, and
with the declared finite node operators $F_i$, $E_i$, $K_h$, $K_d$ of
[[def-level-one-partition-fock-space-and-node-residues]] (the operators act on
*all* partitions). When the wedge bar $\psi$ is supplied by the global-basis
construction, transport it by the formula below; this convention does not
construct that bar. The **symmetric-group model** $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$
is the same $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-vector space with the basis relabelled
$M_\lambda := |\lambda'\rangle$; equivalently, $J : F_{\mathrm{sym}} \to F_{\mathrm{QG}}$
is the $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-linear isomorphism
$$J M_\lambda = |\lambda'\rangle \qquad (\lambda \text{ a partition}),$$
with the field map $q \mapsto q$ (not $q \mapsto q^{-1}$). Transport the
structure along $J$:
$$E_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} E_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad F_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} F_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad K_h^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} K_{\tau h}^{\mathrm{QG}} J \quad (h \in P^\vee), \qquad \psi_{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} \psi J,$$
and give $M_\lambda$ the weight
$\operatorname{wt}(M_\lambda) := \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$. The
transported operators are defined on the ambient basis of *all* partitions.
With $A := \mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$ and the local ring
$A_0 := \{\, f \in \mathbb{Q}(q) : f \text{ is regular at } q = 0 \,\}$, the
**standard chart** of the symmetric-group model is
$$(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}} := \bigoplus_{\lambda} A_0\, M_\lambda ;$$
the full ambient model is indexed by all partitions, while its basic component
in this convention is carried by the $e$-restricted shapes (the comparison with
the QG model is made by the results of this page).

**Label dictionaries and boundaries.** The conjugation map $C : \lambda \mapsto \lambda'$
exchanges the $e$-restricted and the $e$-regular partitions, preserves the
addable/removable *type* of each node and negates residues; it is a comparison
map *between* the restricted and the regular models, not an involution of one
label set, and it is not the same-model sign (Mullineux) involution of
Kleshchev's Theorem 11.8, which fixes the restricted label set and negates
residues along a good-node path. In the symmetric-group regime (ground field of
characteristic $p > 0$, Hecke parameter $\xi = 1$, so that $e = p$ is prime) the
$e$-restricted partitions are the labels of the simple modules in the
dual-Specht convention and the $e$-regular partitions those of James, the two
dictionaries being related by
$D(\lambda) \cong D^{\lambda'} \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$, equivalently
$D^\mu \cong D(\mu') \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$ for $e$-regular $\mu$
([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]);
for a general Hecke parameter the finite integer $e \ge 2$ is its quantum
characteristic (the smallest positive $e$ with $1 + \xi + \dots + \xi^{e-1} = 0$)
and need not be prime, so the general finite-$e$ crystal labels are not called
symmetric-group modules of "characteristic $e$". At quantum characteristic
$e = 0$ (no such positive integer exists, colors $\mathbb{Z}$) no finite affine
datum is present: every level-one partition is a crystal label, and no weight
formula or finite affine statement is made in this boundary.

derivations.claim: The conjugation dictionary identifies the vertex sets of the two components. By [F1] transposition is a bijection from the $e$-restricted onto the $e$-regular partitions, fixing the empty partition, and by [F3] the vertex set of the empty component of the full Fock crystal is exactly the set of $e$-regular partitions. Hence the $J^{-1}$-image of the empty component is exactly the $e$-restricted set, with the empty partition corresponding to the vacuum, and by [F2] the transported modular operators on these labels are the transported normalized Fock operators $\tilde e^{\mathrm{sym}}_i = J^{-1}\tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}J$, $\tilde f^{\mathrm{sym}}_i = J^{-1}\tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}J$.

The transported component is connected and generated from the vacuum. The empty component of [F3] is the canonical $B(\Lambda_0)$, hence connected and generated from its highest vertex by the $\tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}$; transporting along the bijection of step 1.1, the $e$-restricted labels form one connected component of the transported crystal, generated from the empty partition by the operators $\tilde f^{\mathrm{sym}}_i$, that is, by modular cogood additions. In particular every $e$-restricted shape is reached from the empty partition by successive cogood additions, and dually by successive good deletions; for $e = p$ prime this is also the choice-free statement of [F4], whose good and cogood nodes are the modular ones by [F2].

The weight function is the transported one. By [F1] the weight of $M_\lambda$ is $\Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$ with $m_i(\lambda)$ the number of residue-$i$ nodes, and by [F2] it transforms under conjugation as $\operatorname{wt}(\lambda') = \tau(\operatorname{wt}(\lambda))$; the vacuum $\varnothing$ has weight $\Lambda_0$ since $m_i(\varnothing) = 0$. The modular $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ are by construction the numbers of surviving $-$ and $+$, that is, of normal removable and conormal addable $i$-nodes in the sense of the modular signature.

This proves part 1 of the Statement: the empty component of $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$ is exactly the $e$-restricted partitions (step 1.1), its operators are the modular good deletions and cogood additions (step 1.1), its weight is $\Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$ (step 2.2), $\varepsilon$, $\varphi$ count normal and conormal nodes (step 2.2), and it is $B(\Lambda_0)$ with every restricted shape reached from the empty partition by cogood additions (step 2.1).

For part 2, the full $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$ has all partitions as vertices and its module is the transport of the modules of [F3], so its field decomposition is $F_{\mathrm{sym}} \cong \bigoplus_{k\ge0} V(\Lambda_0 - k\delta)^{\oplus p(k)}$ with $p(k)$ ordinary partition numbers; this direct sum is infinite, so $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$ is reducible whenever at least two summands are nonzero (for instance the summands $V(\Lambda_0)$ and $V(\Lambda_0-\delta)$). Since the empty component is exactly the $e$-restricted shapes by step 3.1, every other vertex of the full crystal is a non-restricted shape, and conversely each non-restricted shape lies outside the empty component. The axiom of choice is inherited through [F3], both here for the field decomposition and in steps 1.1-2.1 for the canonical highest-weight-crystal identification. The transport itself introduces no choice. The vertex-set identification and reachability can also be read directly from the choice-free partition-graph supplier of [F2], and [F4] gives the prime-case reachability without choice.

Part 3, the James labels and the socle formula. Let $k$ be of characteristic $p > 0$ and $e = p$; $e$-restricted $\lambda$ are exactly the labels $D(\lambda)$ of the simple $kS_d$-modules in the dual-Specht convention, and for $p$-regular $\lambda'$ the published dictionary gives $D^{\lambda'} \cong D(\lambda) \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$ by [F6]. Suppose $\varepsilon_i(\lambda) > 0$ and let $A$ be the good $i$-node, so that $\tilde e_i\lambda = \lambda \setminus A$ and, by [F5], $\operatorname{soc} E_iD(\lambda) \cong D(\lambda\setminus A)$. Tensoring with $\operatorname{sgn}$ negates the Jucys-Murphy action: for $v \otimes w$ in $M \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$, $L_r(v\otimes w) = \sum_{s<r}((s\,r)v) \otimes ((s\,r)w) = -L_r v \otimes w$ because each $(s\,r)$ acts by $-1$ on $\operatorname{sgn}$ by [F6]; hence the content vector of the sign twist is the negative, and by [F5] the residue summands satisfy $E_{-i}\bigl(M \otimes \operatorname{sgn}\bigr) \cong (E_iM) \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$. The twist is an exact invertible endofunctor (its square is the identity on isomorphism classes), so it preserves socles and simples; applying it to $\operatorname{soc} E_iD(\lambda) \cong D(\lambda\setminus A)$ gives $\operatorname{soc}\bigl(E_{-i}(D(\lambda)\otimes\operatorname{sgn})\bigr) \cong D(\lambda\setminus A) \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$, and the two published re-identifications $D(\lambda)\otimes\operatorname{sgn} \cong D^{\lambda'}$ and $D(\lambda\setminus A)\otimes\operatorname{sgn} \cong D^{(\lambda\setminus A)'}$ of [F6] yield $\operatorname{soc} E_{-i}D^{\lambda'} \cong D^{(\tilde e_i\lambda)'}$; this is the stated formula, and it exhibits $E_{-i}$ as the sign twist of the residue functor $E_i$.

Part 4, the boundary and the naming caveats. At $e = 0$ the colors are $\mathbb{Z}$ and, by [F7] together with the distinct-content computation recorded in the convention item [[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]], each residue class contains at most one corner of a partition, so no signature contains a cancellable pair; every partition reaches the empty partition by good deletions, and the source's restricted set for level $1$ is all partitions. No finite affine datum, charge, weight formula or symmetric-group module statement is made in this boundary; and for a general finite $e \ge 2$ the crystal labels of parts 1 and 2 are Hecke labels, valid for any quantum characteristic $e$, not only for prime $e$ as in part 3.

boundaries.evidence: The empty partition is the highest vertex of the component, reached by zero cogood additions, and step 1.1 identifies it as the J-image of the vacuum.
The quantum-characteristic boundary e = 0 is disposed of separately in step 5.1 and is excluded from the finite affine claims of steps 1.1-4.2.
The level-one constants appear as p(0) = p(1) = 1 in step 4.1's decomposition, and the one-dimensional top weight space is the start of step 2.1.
The prime case includes p = 2, where the sign representation is trivial and -i = i over Z/2, and step 4.2's sign-twist argument covers it without change.
The component's lowest vertex is the vacuum and its full vertex set is identified in step 3.1; every restricted shape is an endpoint of some cogood-addition chain by step 2.1.

The proof inherits AC from F3 in steps 1.1-2.1 for the canonical highest-weight-crystal identification and in step 4.1 for the field decomposition. The explicit transport and combinatorial vertex/reachability calculation add no choices.
One direction of the component identification is step 1.1: every vertex of the empty component transposes to an e-restricted shape.
The converse is step 2.1: every e-restricted shape is generated from the empty partition by cogood additions and hence lies in the component.

citations.quote:
There is an explicit semi-infinite wedge bar $\psi$ with the vacuum fixed,
coefficient bar $q\mapsto q^{-1}$ and $U_q$/bar compatibility, whose restriction
to $M=V(\Lambda_0)$ is the normalized highest module bar. On **all** partitions
its integral triangular correction is

$$G(\lambda)=|\lambda\rangle+\sum_{\mu\ \text{strictly dominated by}\ \lambda}d_{\mu,\lambda}(q)|\mu\rangle, \qquad d_{\mu,\lambda}\in q\mathbb Z[q],$$

with diagonal $1$ and same $e$-core support; the family $\{G(\lambda)\}$ is an
$A$-basis of $F_A$ and an $A_0$-basis of $F_0$, with the actual infinity chart
and balanced $\mathbb Z$-intersection. Exactly the $e$-regular $G(\lambda)$ form
the lower global basis of $M$, identified by the two lower-global-basis
suppliers. The ambient basis is not automatically compatible with the other
field irreducible summands. The transpose equality
$d_{\lambda,\mu}=d_{\mu',\lambda'}$ is **false** in general; the source symmetry
concerns the bar matrix, not $D$. Ambient natural-form dual coefficients use
$(D^{-1})^{\mathsf T}$, and basic upper coefficients require the restricted Gram
inverse and need not be Laurent polynomials.

Fix a finite integer $e \ge 2$. In the symmetric-group convention of
[[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]]:

1. The empty component of the transported full Fock crystal $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$
   is **exactly the set of $e$-restricted partitions**, its operators are the
   modular good-node deletions and cogood-node additions, its weight function is
   $\operatorname{wt}(\lambda) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$, the
   counts $\varepsilon_i$, $\varphi_i$ are the numbers of normal and of
   conormal $i$-nodes, and the component is $B(\Lambda_0)$: every $e$-restricted
   shape is reached from the empty partition by successive cogood additions.
2. The full $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$ has all partitions as vertices and is reducible;
   its transported field decomposition is
   $F_{\mathrm{sym}} \cong \bigoplus_{k \ge 0} V(\Lambda_0 - k\delta)^{\oplus p(k)}$
   with $p(k)$ the number of partitions of $k$, so its other vertices are
   exactly the non-restricted shapes.
3. In the symmetric-group regime (algebraically closed field $k$ of
   characteristic $p > 0$, Hecke parameter $\xi = 1$, so $e = p$ is prime) the
   $e$-restricted labels $\lambda$ are the simple $kS_d$-modules in the
   dual-Specht convention, and for every $i$ with $\varepsilon_i(\lambda) > 0$
   $$\operatorname{soc}\bigl(E_{-i}D^{\lambda'}\bigr) = D^{(\tilde e_i\lambda)'},$$
   where $D^{\lambda'}$ is the James-labelled simple, $E_{-i}$ the
   residue-summand functor after the sign twist, and $D^{(\tilde e_i\lambda)'}$
   the James label of the deleted shape. That is, the standard $E_{-i}$ is the
   residue functor twisted by the sign representation.
4. At quantum characteristic $e = 0$ (colors $\mathbb{Z}$) every level-one
   partition is a label of the empty $\mathfrak{sl}_\infty$ crystal, there are
   no same-content corner cancellations, and no finite affine datum, weight
   formula or Hecke module statement is made.

General finite-$e$ Hecke crystal labels remain valid, but they are not called
symmetric-group modules of "characteristic $e$". The axiom of choice is used
exactly as declared in the contract, through the highest-weight decomposition of
the full Fock module; the vertex-set identification and signature reachability in part 1 are
choice-free. The proof below also uses the declared choice-bearing supplier
to identify the component with the canonical highest-weight crystal.

Fix a finite integer $e \ge 2$ and charge $0$, with the independent-root affine
Cartan datum, its lattices and its diagram reflection $\tau$ fixed as in
[[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]: $I = \mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}$, simple
roots $\alpha_i$, fundamental weights $\Lambda_i$, $\delta$, and
$\tau(i) = -i$. A *node* is a pair $(r,c) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, and
the *residue* of a node is $\operatorname{res}(r,c) := c - r \bmod e$; this is
the level-one, charge-$0$ specialization of the residue used in
[[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]. We use the
English convention (rows increase downwards) and the node language of
[[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]] and
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]].

A partition $\lambda$ is **$e$-regular** if every positive integer occurs as a
part of $\lambda$ fewer than $e$ times, and **$e$-restricted** if
$\lambda_a - \lambda_{a+1} < e$ for every $a \ge 1$, the sequence being padded
by trailing zeros; these are the prime-case notions of
[[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]] with $e$ in place of the prime
$p$. A column of height $e$ is allowed in an $e$-restricted partition. The two
classes are exchanged by conjugation: $\lambda$ is $e$-restricted if and only if
its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular (step 2.1 below).

**The modular (restricted) signature.** Let $\lambda$ be a partition and
$i \in I$. The $i$-nodes of $\lambda$ are its addable and removable nodes of
residue $i$; list them *top to bottom*, that is by increasing row index and then
increasing column index, obtaining $A_1,\dots,A_n$, and form the word
$\sigma = (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m = +$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m = -$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r < s$ with $\sigma_r = -$,
$\sigma_s = +$ and $\sigma_{r+1} = \dots = \sigma_{s-1} = 0$, replace
$\sigma_r,\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies above a $+$. The survivors
are the *normal* removable and *conormal* addable $i$-nodes; write
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda)$ and $\varphi_i(\lambda)$ for their numbers. If
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *good* $i$-node is the removable node
belonging to the first surviving $-$, and $\tilde e_i\lambda := \lambda$ with
that node deleted; if $\varphi_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *cogood* $i$-node is the
addable node belonging to the last surviving $+$, and $\tilde f_i\lambda$ is
$\lambda$ with that node added (otherwise the respective partial operator is
undefined). This is Kleshchev's reduced $i$-signature at charge $0$ and level
one, with good $=$ top normal and cogood $=$ bottom conormal. **This is the
reading used for the restricted (symmetric-group) model**, in which the labels
of the level-one basic module are the $e$-restricted shapes; Fayers' equivalent
formulation reads the list in reverse order, with the opposite cancellation, and extracts the
last surviving $- $ and first surviving $+$, and his increasing-column model of
the $e$-restricted labels is the basic crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$.

**The linear (symmetric-group) model and the transport $J$.** Let
$$F_{\mathrm{QG}} = \bigoplus_{\lambda} \mathbb{Q}(q)\,|\lambda\rangle$$
be the charge-$0$ level-one partition Fock space with
$\operatorname{wt}(|\lambda\rangle) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$,
where $m_i(\lambda)$ is the number of nodes of $[\lambda]$ of residue $i$, and
with the declared finite node operators $F_i$, $E_i$, $K_h$, $K_d$ of
[[def-level-one-partition-fock-space-and-node-residues]] (the operators act on
*all* partitions). When the wedge bar $\psi$ is supplied by the global-basis
construction, transport it by the formula below; this convention does not
construct that bar. The **symmetric-group model** $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$
is the same $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-vector space with the basis relabelled
$M_\lambda := |\lambda'\rangle$; equivalently, $J : F_{\mathrm{sym}} \to F_{\mathrm{QG}}$
is the $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-linear isomorphism
$$J M_\lambda = |\lambda'\rangle \qquad (\lambda \text{ a partition}),$$
with the field map $q \mapsto q$ (not $q \mapsto q^{-1}$). Transport the
structure along $J$:
$$E_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} E_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad F_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} F_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad K_h^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} K_{\tau h}^{\mathrm{QG}} J \quad (h \in P^\vee), \qquad \psi_{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} \psi J,$$
and give $M_\lambda$ the weight
$\operatorname{wt}(M_\lambda) := \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$. The
transported operators are defined on the ambient basis of *all* partitions.
With $A := \mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$ and the local ring
$A_0 := \{\, f \in \mathbb{Q}(q) : f \text{ is regular at } q = 0 \,\}$, the
**standard chart** of the symmetric-group model is
$$(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}} := \bigoplus_{\lambda} A_0\, M_\lambda ;$$
the full ambient model is indexed by all partitions, while its basic component
in this convention is carried by the $e$-restricted shapes (the comparison with
the QG model is made by the results of this page).

**Label dictionaries and boundaries.** The conjugation map $C : \lambda \mapsto \lambda'$
exchanges the $e$-restricted and the $e$-regular partitions, preserves the
addable/removable *type* of each node and negates residues; it is a comparison
map *between* the restricted and the regular models, not an involution of one
label set, and it is not the same-model sign (Mullineux) involution of
Kleshchev's Theorem 11.8, which fixes the restricted label set and negates
residues along a good-node path. In the symmetric-group regime (ground field of
characteristic $p > 0$, Hecke parameter $\xi = 1$, so that $e = p$ is prime) the
$e$-restricted partitions are the labels of the simple modules in the
dual-Specht convention and the $e$-regular partitions those of James, the two
dictionaries being related by
$D(\lambda) \cong D^{\lambda'} \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$, equivalently
$D^\mu \cong D(\mu') \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$ for $e$-regular $\mu$
([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]);
for a general Hecke parameter the finite integer $e \ge 2$ is its quantum
characteristic (the smallest positive $e$ with $1 + \xi + \dots + \xi^{e-1} = 0$)
and need not be prime, so the general finite-$e$ crystal labels are not called
symmetric-group modules of "characteristic $e$". At quantum characteristic
$e = 0$ (no such positive integer exists, colors $\mathbb{Z}$) no finite affine
datum is present: every level-one partition is a crystal label, and no weight
formula or finite affine statement is made in this boundary.

For all partitions $\lambda$ and $\mu$ of the same integer $n$,
$$\lambda\unrhd\mu\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\mu'\unrhd\lambda'.$$

Let $e\ge2$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-abacus configurations as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] and the top-packed set
$X^{(e)}$ of [[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]. For every $\beta$-set $X$
of $\lambda$ the partition $P(X^{(e)})$ is the same, so the $e$-core
$C_e(\lambda)=P(X^{(e)})$ is a well-defined $e$-core partition, and it is
exactly the terminal partition reached by successively removing removable
border strips of size $e$ from $[\lambda]$ until none is left
([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]],
[[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]). In particular every
maximal sequence of such removals gives the same terminal partition
$C_e(\lambda)$, each removed strip has size exactly $e$, and the terminal
partition contains no hook of length $e$. Moreover any two normalised beta-sets
($e\mid|X|$) give the same ordered quotient $Q_e(\lambda)$ and weight.

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, so
that rows are numbered downward and columns rightward, and let
$\nu\subseteq\lambda$ be a subpartition, so that the skew diagram
$[\lambda/\nu]=[\lambda]\setminus[\nu]$ is the set of nodes of $[\lambda]$
outside $[\nu]$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Two nodes are
side-adjacent when their coordinates differ by exactly one in exactly one
coordinate.

A **removable border strip** of $\lambda$ (also called a **skew hook** or
**rim hook**) is a nonempty set $\xi$ of nodes of $[\lambda]$ such that

(i) $\xi$ is **edge-connected**: any two nodes of $\xi$ are joined by a chain
of side-adjacent nodes of $\xi$;

(ii) $\xi$ contains **no $2\times2$ block**: there are no nodes
$(i,j),(i+1,j),(i,j+1),(i+1,j+1)$ all belonging to $\xi$;

(iii) $[\lambda]\setminus\xi$ is again the Young diagram of a partition, say
$[\lambda]\setminus\xi=[\nu]$ for a partition $\nu\vdash n-|\xi|$.

Equivalently, a removable border strip is a skew diagram $\lambda/\nu$ that is
connected and contains no $2\times2$ block; since the complement of
$[\lambda/\nu]$ in $[\lambda]$ is $[\nu]$, condition (iii) is then automatic,
and (i) and (ii) say exactly that the skew diagram is connected and free of
$2\times2$ blocks. We write $\xi=\lambda/\nu$ in that case. The **size** of
$\xi$ is its number of nodes $|\xi|$; a removable border strip of size $r$ is a
**removable $r$-strip**, and then $\nu\vdash n-r$.

The **height** (also **leg length**) of a nonempty connected border strip
$\xi$ is
$$\operatorname{ht}(\xi):=(\text{number of distinct rows of }[\lambda]\text{ occupied by }\xi)-1.$$

**The counting identity.** If a removable border strip $\xi$ has $r$ nodes and
occupies $c$ distinct columns and $w$ distinct rows of $[\lambda]$, then
$w=r-c+1$, hence $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=r-c\ge0$. Indeed $[\lambda/\nu]$ is a
connected, $2\times2$-free skew diagram with complement a Young diagram.
Every strip node $(p,q)$ lies on the rim: if $(p+1,q+1)$ belonged to
$[\lambda]$, it could not belong to $[\nu]$, since that would force
$(p,q)\in[\nu]$; and the partition inequalities then put all four nodes of
the corresponding $2\times2$ block in the strip, a contradiction. The rim
nodes in row $p$ have columns $\max(1,\lambda_{p+1}),\dots,\lambda_p$,
where missing row lengths are zero. Read each such interval from right to
left, then move down at column $\lambda_{p+1}$ to the next row: these are
exactly the rim nodes and their side-adjacencies. Thus the rim is a single
path moving left or down, and its connected subsets are subpaths. The
$r-1$ steps of $\xi$ consist of $w-1$ downward
steps and $c-1$ leftward steps, since the path visits exactly the $w$
occupied rows and exactly the $c$ occupied columns, whence
$r-1=(w-1)+(c-1)$.

In particular $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=0$ exactly when $\xi$ is a horizontal
strip, that is, occupies at most one node in each column, and in general
$c=r-\operatorname{ht}(\xi)$ is the number of columns occupied. A removable
border strip of size $1$ is exactly a removable node
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]): a single node is
edge-connected and contains no $2\times2$ block, and its removal leaves a Young
diagram precisely when the node is removable. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: Finite weight spaces and the ambient form. By [F5] each $V_w$ is finite-dimensional, and $B$ restricts to a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on it with the standard basis orthonormal. The restricted labels $\lambda$ of weight $w$ are finitely many by [F5], so $D_{\mathrm{rect}}$ has finitely many columns, and the corresponding $G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda)$ are linearly independent because they are distinct elements of the lower global basis of $M_{\mathrm{sym}}$ from [F2] (respectively the defining family of [F1] transported).

Support of the transition polynomials. By [F1], $d_{(\lambda,\lambda)}=1$, all off-diagonal coefficients lie in $q\mathbb Z[q]$, and a nonzero off-diagonal coefficient requires $\mu'$ to be strictly dominated by $\lambda'$ with the same $e$-core. By [F6] this dominance condition is equivalent to $\mu$ strictly dominating $\lambda$. Transposition preserves side adjacency, size and $2	imes2$ blocks, and carries the partition complement of a border strip to its transposed complement. It therefore bijects maximal sequences of $e$-strip removals, so uniqueness in [F7] gives $C_e(
u')=C_e(
u)'$ for every partition $
u$. Applying this to $\lambda,\mu$ transports the same-core condition. For weight support, the $U$/bar compatibility of [F1] gives $\psi K_h=K_{-h}\psi$; since $\psi$ sends $q$ to $q^{-1}$, a weight vector $v$ of weight $w$ satisfies $K_h\psi v=q^{\langle w,hangle}\psi v$. Thus the bar preserves each weight space, and its triangular correction recursion does too. Each $|\mu'angle$ occurring in $G_{\mathrm{QG}}(\lambda')$ consequently has the same full affine weight as $|\lambda'angle$. Independence of the simple roots gives $m_j(\mu')=m_j(\lambda')$ for every $j$; the reflected weight of $\mu$ equals that of $\lambda$.

The ambient upper coordinates. Let $D:=D_{\mathrm{rect}}$, with $D_{\mu\lambda}=d_{(\lambda,\mu)}$. The matrix $H=D^{\mathsf t}D$ is the Gram matrix of the basic lower vectors under the ambient orthonormal form. Since $D(0)$ has distinct coordinate columns, $H(0)=I$ by [F5], proving $\det H\ne0$. The columns of $DH^{-1}$ lie in the column space of $D$, namely $(M_{\mathrm{sym}})_w$, and $(DH^{-1})^{\mathsf t}D=H^{-1}H=I$, so they pair as the dual family. Nondegeneracy of $H$ makes this family unique inside the basic subspace. In the whole ambient space the pairing equations determine a coset modulo the orthogonal complement of the basic subspace. The coefficients $e_{(\lambda,\mu)}=(DH^{-1})_{\mu\lambda}$ are in $\mathbb Q(q)$.

The worked instance at $e=2$. The weight space contains the standard shapes $(2),(1,1)$, with $(1,1)$ the only restricted label. On the QG side the node formulas give $F_0|\varnothing\rangle=|1\rangle$ and $F_1|1\rangle=|2\rangle+q|11\rangle$: the top addable $1$-node has no corner to its right, while the bottom addable $1$-node has the top addable node to its right. This vector is bar-fixed because the vacuum and the lowering generators are bar-fixed by [F1], and it is congruent to $|2\rangle$ modulo $qF_0$. Uniqueness in [F1] therefore gives $G(2)=|2\rangle+q|11\rangle$. Applying $J^{-1}$ yields $G_{\mathrm{sym}}(1,1)=M_{1,1}+qM_2$. With rows $(2),(1,1)$, $D_{\mathrm{rect}}=\binom q1$, $H=1+q^2$, and step 2.2 gives $G_{\mathrm{sym}}^*(1,1)=(qM_2^*+M_{1,1}^*)/(1+q^2)$. The coefficient $1/(1+q^2)$ is not Laurent integral: a Laurent polynomial can have a finite pole only at $0$, whereas this rational function has poles at the nonzero roots of $1+q^2$.

The full ambient dual matrix. On the whole Fock space, $D_{\mathrm{full}}$ is unitriangular by [F1] with off-diagonal entries in $q\mathbb{Z}[q]$; its dual basis with respect to the ambient form $B$ has coefficient matrix the transpose inverse $D_{\mathrm{full}}^{-\mathsf{t}}$, by the same computation as step 2.2 applied to the square unitriangular matrix (here the standard basis of the whole space is orthonormal and the family $\{G(\mu)\}$ is a basis). We claim $D_{\mathrm{full}}^{-1}$ has entries in $\mathbb{Z}[q]$: in every finite truncation the strictly triangular part $N$ of $D_{\mathrm{full}} = 1 + N$ satisfies $N^{m} = 0$ for large $m$, so $(1+N)^{-1} = 1 - N + N^2 - \dots$ is a finite sum with entries in $\mathbb{Z}[q]$; hence $D_{\mathrm{full}}^{-\mathsf{t}}$ is Laurent integral, in contrast with the non-integral ambient coordinates of step 3.1.

classes are exchanged by conjugation: $\lambda$ is $e$-restricted if and only if
its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular (step 2.1 below).

residue $i$; list them *top to bottom*, that is by increasing row index and then
increasing column index, obtaining $A_1,\dots,A_n$, and form the word
$\sigma = (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m = +$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m = -$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r < s$ with $\sigma_r = -$,

$\sigma_r,\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies above a $+$. The survivors

$\varepsilon_i(\lambda)$ and $\varphi_i(\lambda)$ for their numbers. If
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *good* $i$-node is the removable node
belonging to the first surviving $-$, and $\tilde e_i\lambda := \lambda$ with
that node deleted; if $\varphi_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *cogood* $i$-node is the
addable node belonging to the last surviving $+$, and $\tilde f_i\lambda$ is
$\lambda$ with that node added (otherwise the respective partial operator is
undefined). This is Kleshchev's reduced $i$-signature at charge $0$ and level
one, with good $=$ top normal and cogood $=$ bottom conormal. **This is the
reading used for the restricted (symmetric-group) model**, in which the labels
of the level-one basic module are the $e$-restricted shapes; Fayers' equivalent
formulation reads the list in reverse order, with the opposite cancellation, and extracts the
last surviving $- $ and first surviving $+$, and his increasing-column model of
the $e$-restricted labels is the basic crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$.

$$F_{\mathrm{QG}} = \bigoplus_{\lambda} \mathbb{Q}(q)\,|\lambda\rangle$$
be the charge-$0$ level-one partition Fock space with
$\operatorname{wt}(|\lambda\rangle) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$,
where $m_i(\lambda)$ is the number of nodes of $[\lambda]$ of residue $i$, and
with the declared finite node operators $F_i$, $E_i$, $K_h$, $K_d$ of
[[def-level-one-partition-fock-space-and-node-residues]] (the operators act on
*all* partitions). When the wedge bar $\psi$ is supplied by the global-basis
construction, transport it by the formula below; this convention does not
construct that bar. The **symmetric-group model** $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$
is the same $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-vector space with the basis relabelled
$M_\lambda := |\lambda'\rangle$; equivalently, $J : F_{\mathrm{sym}} \to F_{\mathrm{QG}}$
is the $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-linear isomorphism
$$J M_\lambda = |\lambda'\rangle \qquad (\lambda \text{ a partition}),$$
with the field map $q \mapsto q$ (not $q \mapsto q^{-1}$). Transport the
structure along $J$:
$$E_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} E_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad F_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} F_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad K_h^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} K_{\tau h}^{\mathrm{QG}} J \quad (h \in P^\vee), \qquad \psi_{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} \psi J,$$
and give $M_\lambda$ the weight
$\operatorname{wt}(M_\lambda) := \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$. The
transported operators are defined on the ambient basis of *all* partitions.
With $A := \mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$ and the local ring
$A_0 := \{\, f \in \mathbb{Q}(q) : f \text{ is regular at } q = 0 \,\}$, the
**standard chart** of the symmetric-group model is
$$(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}} := \bigoplus_{\lambda} A_0\, M_\lambda ;$$
the full ambient model is indexed by all partitions, while its basic component
in this convention is carried by the $e$-restricted shapes (the comparison with
the QG model is made by the results of this page).

exchanges the $e$-restricted and the $e$-regular partitions, preserves the
addable/removable *type* of each node and negates residues; it is a comparison
map *between* the restricted and the regular models, not an involution of one
label set, and it is not the same-model sign (Mullineux) involution of
Kleshchev's Theorem 11.8, which fixes the restricted label set and negates
residues along a good-node path. In the symmetric-group regime (ground field of
characteristic $p > 0$, Hecke parameter $\xi = 1$, so that $e = p$ is prime) the
$e$-restricted partitions are the labels of the simple modules in the
dual-Specht convention and the $e$-regular partitions those of James, the two

$D^\mu \cong D(\mu') \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$ for $e$-regular $\mu$

for a general Hecke parameter the finite integer $e \ge 2$ is its quantum
characteristic (the smallest positive $e$ with $1 + \xi + \dots + \xi^{e-1} = 0$)
and need not be prime, so the general finite-$e$ crystal labels are not called
symmetric-group modules of "characteristic $e$". At quantum characteristic

datum is present: every level-one partition is a crystal label, and no weight
formula or finite affine statement is made in this boundary.

higher. For an addable $i$-node $\gamma$ of $\lambda$ (so that
$\mu=\lambda+\gamma$) define

$$N_i^r(\lambda,\gamma):=\#\{\text{addable }i\text{-nodes of }\lambda\text{ with content}>\text{content}(\gamma)\}-\#\{\text{removable }i\text{-nodes of }\lambda\text{ with content}>\text{content}(\gamma)\},$$

$\lambda=\mu-\gamma$) define $N_i^l(\lambda,\mu)$ by the same formula inside the
smaller diagram $\lambda=\mu-\gamma$ with $>$ replaced by $<$, always excluding
$\gamma$ itself. The node formulas are then

$$F_i|\lambda\rangle=\sum_{\gamma}q^{N_i^r(\lambda,\gamma)}|\lambda+\gamma\rangle,\qquad E_i|\mu\rangle=\sum_{\gamma}q^{-N_i^l(\mu-\gamma,\mu)}|\mu-\gamma\rangle,$$

content order just fixed, and it is used to define the finite signature
selection: a Chevalley coefficient minimiser is not in general a Kashiwara
arrow, and even a nonzero single Chevalley term can have zero crystal arrow.

The constructed node operators on **all** partition vectors make the charge-$0$
partition Fock space $F$ into a $P$-graded integrable module for
$U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_e)$ with the fixed coproduct and the cyclic Cartan
datum: all toral commutation rules and mixed commutators
$[E_i,F_j]=\delta_{ij}(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$ hold, and both quantum Serre
sums vanish, including the cubic $e=2$ case with
$a_{01}=a_{10}=-2$ and $[3]=q^2+1+q^{-2}$. Each color acts on finite Boolean
cubes, and $F_i,E_i$ change the $P$-weight by $\mp\alpha_i$. Ordinary standard
coefficients may have $q^{-1}$ poles; normalized Kashiwara lattice stability is
a separate statement.

Consider the modular reading on the one hand (the top-to-bottom residue
signature with good $=$ first surviving $-$ and cogood $=$ last surviving $+$ of
[[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]], whose
operators delete the good node and add the cogood node on $e$-restricted
labels) and the level-one Fock crystal $\tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_i$,
$\tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}_i$ on the other. Conjugation
$C(\lambda) = \lambda'$ sends the modular operators on $e$-restricted
partitions onto the normalized operators of the **empty connected component** of
the QG full partition Fock crystal, with the colors negated:
$$C\,\tilde e_i\lambda = \tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}C\lambda, \qquad C\,\tilde f_i\lambda = \tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}C\lambda \qquad (\lambda\ e\text{-restricted}),$$
including the zero values: the left side is zero exactly when the right side is.
The survivor counts are the same on both sides,
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda) = \varepsilon_{-i}(\lambda')$ and
$\varphi_i(\lambda) = \varphi_{-i}(\lambda')$, and the weight transforms by the
diagram reflection, $\operatorname{wt}(\lambda') = \tau(\operatorname{wt}(\lambda))$.
With the transported full module $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$ of
[[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]], the
modular signatures likewise give its normalized operators on **all** partitions
(the transported operators $J^{-1}\tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}J$,
$J^{-1}\tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}J$), and the restricted subset of that full
crystal is its basic component. In both conventions good means removable
(deletion, $\tilde e$) and cogood means addable (addition, $\tilde f$): there is
no opposite naming-polarity dictionary exchanging deletion with addition.
Ordinary Chevalley coefficients, especially negative powers such as $q^{-1}$,
do not define these arrows.

Fix a finite integer $e \ge 2$ and charge $0$, with the independent-root affine
Cartan datum, its lattices and its diagram reflection $\tau$ fixed as in
[[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]: $I = \mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}$, simple
roots $\alpha_i$, fundamental weights $\Lambda_i$, $\delta$, and
$\tau(i) = -i$. A *node* is a pair $(r,c) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, and
the *residue* of a node is $\operatorname{res}(r,c) := c - r \bmod e$; this is
the level-one, charge-$0$ specialization of the residue used in
[[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]. We use the
English convention (rows increase downwards) and the node language of
[[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]] and
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]].

A partition $\lambda$ is **$e$-regular** if every positive integer occurs as a
part of $\lambda$ fewer than $e$ times, and **$e$-restricted** if
$\lambda_a - \lambda_{a+1} < e$ for every $a \ge 1$, the sequence being padded
by trailing zeros; these are the prime-case notions of
[[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]] with $e$ in place of the prime
$p$. A column of height $e$ is allowed in an $e$-restricted partition. The two
classes are exchanged by conjugation: $\lambda$ is $e$-restricted if and only if
its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular (step 2.1 below).

**The modular (restricted) signature.** Let $\lambda$ be a partition and
$i \in I$. The $i$-nodes of $\lambda$ are its addable and removable nodes of
residue $i$; list them *top to bottom*, that is by increasing row index and then
increasing column index, obtaining $A_1,\dots,A_n$, and form the word
$\sigma = (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m = +$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m = -$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r < s$ with $\sigma_r = -$,
$\sigma_s = +$ and $\sigma_{r+1} = \dots = \sigma_{s-1} = 0$, replace
$\sigma_r,\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies above a $+$. The survivors
are the *normal* removable and *conormal* addable $i$-nodes; write
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda)$ and $\varphi_i(\lambda)$ for their numbers. If
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *good* $i$-node is the removable node
belonging to the first surviving $-$, and $\tilde e_i\lambda := \lambda$ with
that node deleted; if $\varphi_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *cogood* $i$-node is the
addable node belonging to the last surviving $+$, and $\tilde f_i\lambda$ is
$\lambda$ with that node added (otherwise the respective partial operator is
undefined). This is Kleshchev's reduced $i$-signature at charge $0$ and level
one, with good $=$ top normal and cogood $=$ bottom conormal. **This is the
reading used for the restricted (symmetric-group) model**, in which the labels
of the level-one basic module are the $e$-restricted shapes; Fayers' equivalent
formulation reads the list in reverse order, with the opposite cancellation, and extracts the
last surviving $- $ and first surviving $+$, and his increasing-column model of
the $e$-restricted labels is the basic crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$.

**The linear (symmetric-group) model and the transport $J$.** Let
$$F_{\mathrm{QG}} = \bigoplus_{\lambda} \mathbb{Q}(q)\,|\lambda\rangle$$
be the charge-$0$ level-one partition Fock space with
$\operatorname{wt}(|\lambda\rangle) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$,
where $m_i(\lambda)$ is the number of nodes of $[\lambda]$ of residue $i$, and
with the declared finite node operators $F_i$, $E_i$, $K_h$, $K_d$ of
[[def-level-one-partition-fock-space-and-node-residues]] (the operators act on
*all* partitions). When the wedge bar $\psi$ is supplied by the global-basis
construction, transport it by the formula below; this convention does not
construct that bar. The **symmetric-group model** $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$
is the same $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-vector space with the basis relabelled
$M_\lambda := |\lambda'\rangle$; equivalently, $J : F_{\mathrm{sym}} \to F_{\mathrm{QG}}$
is the $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-linear isomorphism
$$J M_\lambda = |\lambda'\rangle \qquad (\lambda \text{ a partition}),$$
with the field map $q \mapsto q$ (not $q \mapsto q^{-1}$). Transport the
structure along $J$:
$$E_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} E_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad F_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} F_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad K_h^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} K_{\tau h}^{\mathrm{QG}} J \quad (h \in P^\vee), \qquad \psi_{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} \psi J,$$
and give $M_\lambda$ the weight
$\operatorname{wt}(M_\lambda) := \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$. The
transported operators are defined on the ambient basis of *all* partitions.
With $A := \mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$ and the local ring
$A_0 := \{\, f \in \mathbb{Q}(q) : f \text{ is regular at } q = 0 \,\}$, the
**standard chart** of the symmetric-group model is
$$(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}} := \bigoplus_{\lambda} A_0\, M_\lambda ;$$
the full ambient model is indexed by all partitions, while its basic component
in this convention is carried by the $e$-restricted shapes (the comparison with
the QG model is made by the results of this page).

**Label dictionaries and boundaries.** The conjugation map $C : \lambda \mapsto \lambda'$
exchanges the $e$-restricted and the $e$-regular partitions, preserves the
addable/removable *type* of each node and negates residues; it is a comparison
map *between* the restricted and the regular models, not an involution of one
label set, and it is not the same-model sign (Mullineux) involution of
Kleshchev's Theorem 11.8, which fixes the restricted label set and negates
residues along a good-node path. In the symmetric-group regime (ground field of
characteristic $p > 0$, Hecke parameter $\xi = 1$, so that $e = p$ is prime) the
$e$-restricted partitions are the labels of the simple modules in the
dual-Specht convention and the $e$-regular partitions those of James, the two
dictionaries being related by
$D(\lambda) \cong D^{\lambda'} \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$, equivalently
$D^\mu \cong D(\mu') \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$ for $e$-regular $\mu$
([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]);
for a general Hecke parameter the finite integer $e \ge 2$ is its quantum
characteristic (the smallest positive $e$ with $1 + \xi + \dots + \xi^{e-1} = 0$)
and need not be prime, so the general finite-$e$ crystal labels are not called
symmetric-group modules of "characteristic $e$". At quantum characteristic
$e = 0$ (no such positive integer exists, colors $\mathbb{Z}$) no finite affine
datum is present: every level-one partition is a crystal label, and no weight
formula or finite affine statement is made in this boundary.

With the declared use of the Axiom of Choice in the general integrable-module
decomposition, the empty connected component of the full partition crystal of
[[thm-the-crystal-of-level-one-fock-space-is-the-good-node-partition-graph]] is
the canonical highest weight crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$, with exactly the
$e$-regular labels. Its module is $M=U_q(\mathfrak g)|\varnothing\rangle$ and
its lower $A_0$-lattice is $M\cap F_0$; it occurs once. More precisely

$$F=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}V(\Lambda_0-k\delta)^{\oplus p(k)},$$

a locally weight-finite indexed direct sum in which $p(k)$ is the number of
ordinary partitions of $k$; consequently
$\mathrm{ch}\,F=\mathrm{ch}\,V(\Lambda_0)\prod_{r\ge1}(1-e^{-r\delta})^{-1}$.
A highest **crystal** label need not be a highest **field** standard vector, and
the ambient canonical basis need not split these summands.

**Assume the axiom of choice** ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $M$ be a chosen $P$-graded type-one quantum weight module that is integrable, has finite-dimensional label-weight spaces and weight set contained in a finite union of cones $\lambda-Q_+$ ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]), and let $(L,B)$ be a crystal basis of $M$ ([[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]).

(i) **Splitting along the top isotypic part.** Let $\lambda$ be a maximal weight of $M$, put $N_0:=U_q(\mathfrak g)M_\lambda$ and let $N_1$ be the sum of the remaining simple constituents, so that $M=N_0\oplus N_1$ and $N_0\cong V(\lambda)^{\oplus m}$ with $m=\dim M_\lambda$. Then $L=(L\cap N_0)\oplus(L\cap N_1)$, $B=\bigl(B\cap(L\cap N_0)/q(L\cap N_0)\bigr)\sqcup\bigl(B\cap(L\cap N_1)/q(L\cap N_1)\bigr)$, and both pairs are crystal bases of $N_0$ and $N_1$.

(ii) **Uniqueness.** There is a locally weight-finite indexed family $(\lambda_j)_{j\in J}$ in $P^+$ and an isomorphism of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-modules $\Phi:M\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\bigoplus_{j\in J}V(\lambda_j)$ with $\Phi(L)=\bigoplus_j\mathcal L(\lambda_j)$ and $\Phi$ inducing a bijection $B\to\bigsqcup_j\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$ of crystals. The multiset $\{\lambda_j:j\in J\}$ is the multiset of highest weights of the simple integrable constituents of $M$: the number of $j$ with $\lambda_j=\lambda$ equals the multiplicity $[M:V(\lambda)]$.

(iii) **Components.** Through $\Phi$ the connected components of the crystal $B$ are exactly the canonical highest weight crystals $\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$; each component has a unique highest weight element $b$, of dominant weight $\lambda$, and equals the lowering-generated subcrystal $F(b)$ of [[def-highest-weight-element-and-connected-highest-weight-crystal]]. In particular the crystal graph of any crystal basis of $M$ is determined up to isomorphism by $M$, and no other highest weight elements occur.

**Choice.** The axiom of choice is declared in [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and used to obtain the decomposition of $M$ into simple integrable highest weight modules from [[prop-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-modules-are-semisimple]], which selects a maximal independent family of simple submodules simultaneously. It also permits simultaneous choices of lifts of the finite residue bases in the possibly infinite family of top spaces. After those choices, each lattice and crystal argument is finite and choice-free. No incompatible-axiom branch is used, and no global $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-freeness is assumed. The index set $J$ need not be finite in affine or indefinite type; local weight finiteness means only finitely many summands contribute to any fixed label-weight space.

There is an explicit semi-infinite wedge bar $\psi$ with the vacuum fixed,
coefficient bar $q\mapsto q^{-1}$ and $U_q$/bar compatibility, whose restriction
to $M=V(\Lambda_0)$ is the normalized highest module bar. On **all** partitions
its integral triangular correction is

$$G(\lambda)=|\lambda\rangle+\sum_{\mu\ \text{strictly dominated by}\ \lambda}d_{\mu,\lambda}(q)|\mu\rangle, \qquad d_{\mu,\lambda}\in q\mathbb Z[q],$$

with diagonal $1$ and same $e$-core support; the family $\{G(\lambda)\}$ is an
$A$-basis of $F_A$ and an $A_0$-basis of $F_0$, with the actual infinity chart
and balanced $\mathbb Z$-intersection. Exactly the $e$-regular $G(\lambda)$ form
the lower global basis of $M$, identified by the two lower-global-basis
suppliers. The ambient basis is not automatically compatible with the other
field irreducible summands. The transpose equality
$d_{\lambda,\mu}=d_{\mu',\lambda'}$ is **false** in general; the source symmetry
concerns the bar matrix, not $D$. Ambient natural-form dual coefficients use
$(D^{-1})^{\mathsf T}$, and basic upper coefficients require the restricted Gram
inverse and need not be Laurent polynomials.

derivations.claim: For a partition $\lambda$, list addable pluses and removable minuses of residue $i$ from top to bottom and cancel $-+$ pairs by a last-in-first-out minus stack. Deleting the first surviving minus and adding the last surviving plus are inverse selected moves. Indeed changing the selected corner changes its sign; every other altered boundary corner has residue $i+1$ or $i-1$, different from $i$ even at $e=2$. Immediately before a first surviving minus the minus stack is empty, and every suffix prefix has at least as many remaining minus pushes as plus pops. After flipping that minus to plus, these conditions say precisely that this plus survives and no later plus does. Reversing the flip proves the converse. This retains the positions of the selected signs, not just their counts.

Good deletion preserves restrictedness. For a removable row $r$, only its gap and the gap immediately above can change: the former decreases by one and the latter increases by one. The only possible violation is $r>1$ and $\lambda_{r-1}-\lambda_r=e-1$. Then the removable corners in rows $r-1,r$ have equal residues, and their minus signs are adjacent in that residue word: the addable corners between them have residues differing by one. If the lower minus survives, the upper one also survives, since stack pops remove the lower minus first. The lower one therefore cannot be the first surviving minus. Cogood addition preserves restrictedness by the dual adjacent-plus argument: if its row gap were $e-1$, the later same-residue addable corner would survive whenever the earlier one did, contradicting selection of the last surviving plus. Hence step 1.1 gives inverse partial operations on the restricted vertex set.

Every nonempty restricted partition has a good deletion. Let $h$ be its height. Its bottom removable node has residue $\lambda_h-h$, while the only boundary node below it is the addable $(h+1,1)$ of residue $-h$. The difference $\lambda_h$ lies strictly between zero and $e$, so these residues differ. There is consequently no later same-residue plus to cancel that bottom minus. At least one minus survives in that residue, and its first surviving minus is a good node. By step 2.1 its deletion stays restricted. Repeating decreases the number of boxes and ends at the empty diagram; reversing gives cogood additions by step 1.1. All selections may be made by the least residue and then the prescribed extremal sign, using finite sets.
